## 3. The pole-order theorem

Fix a finite index set $S$ with $|S| = m$ and a family $(f_i)_{i \in S}$ of
normalized series. Write $P = \prod_{i \in S} f_i$.

**Theorem 3.1 (Leading coefficient).** $\operatorname{lc}(P) = 1$.

*Proof sketch.* Induction on $|S|$ using multiplicativity of the leading
coefficient (Lemma 2.3) and $\operatorname{lc}(f_i) = 1$ (Lemma 2.7); the empty
product has leading coefficient $1$. $\square$

**Corollary 3.2.** $P \ne 0$.

*Proof sketch.* The zero series has no leading coefficient equal to $1$; more
carefully, if $P = 0$ then $P$ has no nonzero coefficient at all, contradicting
Theorem 3.1. $\square$

**Theorem 3.3 (Pole-Order Theorem).**
$$\operatorname{ord}\Big(\prod_{i \in S} f_i\Big) = -m,
\qquad m = |S|.$$
Equivalently, $P = q^{-m} + (\text{higher order terms})$.

*Proof sketch.* By Lemma 2.4 the order of $P$ is $\sum_{i \in S}
\operatorname{ord}(f_i) = \sum_{i \in S}(-1) = -m$, using Lemma 2.7. Corollary
3.2 guarantees the value is finite, so the statement is meaningful as an equality
of integers. Combined with Theorem 3.1, the expansion begins with $1 \cdot
q^{-m}$. $\square$

The content of Theorem 3.3 is the word *exactly*: no cancellation is possible.
Poles of normalized series add up with perfect fidelity because the leading
coefficients are all $1$ and $\mathbb{C}$ is a domain.

**Theorem 3.4 (Non-Closure).** $P$ is normalized if and only if $m = 1$.

*Proof sketch.* If $P$ is normalized then $\operatorname{ord}(P) = -1$ by Lemma
2.7, while $\operatorname{ord}(P) = -m$ by Theorem 3.3; hence $m = 1$.
Conversely if $m = 1$ then $P = f_i$ for the unique $i \in S$, which is
normalized by hypothesis. $\square$

**Theorem 3.5 (Genuine pole).** If $m \ge 1$ then $P \notin \mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$,
i.e. $P$ is not the image of any formal power series.

*Proof sketch.* By Theorems 3.1 and 3.3 the coefficient of $q^{-m}$ in $P$ is
$1$. Any element of the image of $\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$ has vanishing
coefficients in all negative degrees, and $-m < 0$. $\square$

So the obstruction is not an inconvenience of presentation: the product lies
outside the power series ring as a matter of fact.

---

## 4. Correcting the pole, and the uniqueness of the correction

**Theorem 4.1 (Unique monomial correction).** For $k \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$,
$$\operatorname{ord}\Big(q^{k}\prod_{i \in S} f_i\Big) = 0
\iff k = m.$$
In particular $\operatorname{ord}\big(q^{m}\prod_i f_i\big) = 0$.

*Proof sketch.* $\operatorname{ord}(q^k) = k$, and by Lemma 2.4 and Theorem 3.3
the order of the corrected product is $k - m$; this vanishes iff $k = m$.
$\square$

**Theorem 4.2 (Leading coefficient survives).**
$\operatorname{lc}\big(q^m \prod_i f_i\big) = 1$; equivalently, the constant term
of the corrected series is $1$.

*Proof sketch.* Multiplicativity of $\operatorname{lc}$ together with
$\operatorname{lc}(q^m) = 1$ and Theorem 3.1. Since the order is $0$ by Theorem
4.1, the leading coefficient *is* the constant term. $\square$

**Definition 4.3 (Unit part).** For normalized $f$, define $U(f) \in
\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$ to be the power series with $U(f)_n = f_{n-1}$, $n \ge 0$;
by construction $q f = U(f)$ as Laurent series and $U(f)_0 = f_{-1} = 1$,
$U(f)_1 = f_0$, $U(f)_2 = f_1$, and in general $U(f)_n = f_{n-1}$.

**Theorem 4.4 (Unit structure of the corrected product).** For normalized
$(f_i)_{i \in S}$,
$$q^{m}\prod_{i \in S} f_i \;=\; \prod_{i \in S} U(f_i)
\quad\text{in } \mathbb{C}[\![q]\!],$$
and this power series is a **unit** of $\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$.

*Proof sketch.* Each $U(f_i) = q f_i$, so $\prod_i U(f_i) = q^{m}\prod_i f_i$.
Each $U(f_i)$ has constant term $1$, hence is a unit by Lemma 2.5; a finite
product of units is a unit. $\square$

Theorem 4.4 upgrades Theorem 4.1 from a numerical statement ("the order is $0$")
to a structural one: after correction the product does not merely land in the
ring $\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$; it lands in the group $\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]^{\times}$,
indeed in the subgroup $1 + q\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$ of principal units.

---

## 5. Unique factorization of normalized series

**Theorem 5.1 (Structure theorem).** For each normalized $f$ there is a
*unique* power series $u$ with constant term $1$ such that
$$f = q^{-1} \cdot u .$$
Namely $u = U(f)$.

*Proof sketch.* *Existence:* $q^{-1}U(f) = q^{-1}(qf) = f$, and $U(f)_0 =
f_{-1} = 1$. *Uniqueness:* if $f = q^{-1}v$ with $v \in \mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$,
multiply by $q$ (a unit of the field $\mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)$) to get $v = qf =
U(f)$; since $\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!] \to \mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)$ is injective, $v$ and
$U(f)$ agree as power series. $\square$

**Corollary 5.2 (Factorization of the product).** For normalized
$(f_i)_{i \in S}$ with $|S| = m$,
$$\prod_{i \in S} f_i \;=\; q^{-m}\cdot \prod_{i \in S} U(f_i),$$
a monomial of degree $-m$ times a unit of $\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$ with constant
term $1$.

Corollary 5.2 is the conceptual root of the whole paper. Once one knows that the
normalized series are exactly the elements $q^{-1} u$ with $u \in 1 +
q\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$, everything else is bookkeeping in the direct product
decomposition
$$\mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)^{\times} \;\cong\; q^{\mathbb{Z}} \times
\mathbb{C}^{\times} \times \big(1 + q\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]\big),$$
under which $\mathcal{N}$ is the slice $\{q^{-1}\}\times\{1\}\times(1 +
q\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!])$. Multiplying $m$ elements of the slice multiplies the
monomial components, sending $q^{-1} \mapsto q^{-m}$; the slice is closed under
multiplication only if $m = 1$, because $\{-1\}$ is closed under addition in
$\mathbb{Z}$ only for one-fold sums.

---

## 6. The valuation as a group homomorphism

Restricting the order to the multiplicative group of the field packages the
obstruction group-theoretically.

**Lemma 6.1.** For nonzero $x, y \in \mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)$,
$\operatorname{ord}(xy) = \operatorname{ord}(x) + \operatorname{ord}(y)$ in
$\mathbb{Z}$, and $\operatorname{ord}(1) = 0$.

**Theorem 6.2 (Order homomorphism).** The map
$$\operatorname{ord} \colon \mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)^{\times} \longrightarrow
\mathbb{Z}$$
is a surjective group homomorphism from the multiplicative group of the field of
Laurent series onto the additive group of integers.

*Proof sketch.* Homomorphism: Lemma 6.1 (every nonzero element of a field is a
unit, so the domain is all of $\mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)\setminus\{0\}$). Surjectivity:
for $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ the monomial $q^{k}$ is invertible with inverse $q^{-k}$,
and $\operatorname{ord}(q^k) = k$. $\square$

**Lemma 6.3.** Every normalized series is a unit of $\mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)$, and
$\operatorname{ord}(f) = -1$: normalized series lie in the fibre
$\operatorname{ord}^{-1}(-1)$.

**Corollary 6.4 (Completeness of the obstruction).** A product of $m$ normalized
series lies in the fibre $\operatorname{ord}^{-1}(-m)$, hence — the fibres of a
homomorphism being pairwise disjoint — in no other fibre. In particular it lies
in $\operatorname{ord}^{-1}(-1)$, the fibre containing all normalized series, if
and only if $m = 1$.

This is the sense in which the pole order is a *complete* obstruction rather
than a mere necessary condition: it is the value of a homomorphism, and
homomorphism values partition the group. The kernel
$\operatorname{ord}^{-1}(0) = \mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]^{\times}$ is exactly the group
of unit power series, so Corollary 5.2 exhibits the standard splitting: every
nonzero Laurent series is a monomial times an element of the kernel, uniquely.

---

## 7. Newton-type identities for the coefficients past the pole

Corollary 5.2 transfers all coefficient questions about $\prod_i f_i$ to
coefficient questions about a product of power series with constant term $1$.
Concretely, for $k \ge 0$,
$$\Big(\prod_{i \in S} f_i\Big)_{k - m} \;=\; \Big(\prod_{i \in S} U(f_i)\Big)_{k}.$$
Write $f_i = q^{-1} + a_i + b_i q + \cdots$, so $U(f_i) = 1 + a_i q + b_i q^2 +
\cdots$.

**Lemma 7.1 (Level 1 for unit power series).** If $(g_i)_{i \in S}$ are power
series with $(g_i)_0 = 1$ for all $i$, then
$$\Big(\prod_{i \in S} g_i\Big)_1 = \sum_{i \in S} (g_i)_1 .$$

*Proof sketch.* Induction on $|S|$, using $(gh)_1 = g_0 h_1 + g_1 h_0$ and the
fact that a product of series with constant term $1$ again has constant term $1$.
$\square$

**Theorem 7.2 (Subleading Laurent coefficient).** For normalized
$(f_i)_{i \in S}$ with $|S| = m$,
$$\Big(\prod_{i \in S} f_i\Big)_{1-m} \;=\; \sum_{i \in S} a_i,$$
the sum of the constant terms of the factors.

*Proof sketch.* Apply the coefficient transfer with $k = 1$ and Lemma 7.1 to
$g_i = U(f_i)$, noting $(U(f_i))_1 = a_i$. $\square$

**Lemma 7.3 (Level 2 for unit power series).** If $(g_i)_{i \in S}$ are power
series with $(g_i)_0 = 1$, then
$$2\Big(\prod_{i \in S} g_i\Big)_2
= 2\sum_{i \in S} (g_i)_2 + \Big(\sum_{i \in S} (g_i)_1\Big)^{2}
- \sum_{i \in S} (g_i)_1^{2}.$$

*Proof sketch.* Induction on $|S|$. The inductive step uses the convolution
formula $(gh)_2 = g_0 h_2 + g_1 h_1 + g_2 h_0$ together with $g_0 = h_0 = 1$,
the level-1 identity of Lemma 7.1 for the partial product, and the algebraic
identity $\big(A + x\big)^2 - \big(A^2 + x^2\big) = 2Ax$. The statement is
written in denominator-free form to avoid dividing by $2$; equivalently
$\big(\prod g_i\big)_2 = \sum_i (g_i)_2 + e_2\big((g_i)_1\big)$ where
$e_2(x) = \sum_{i<j} x_i x_j$, since $\big(\sum x_i\big)^2 - \sum x_i^2 =
2 e_2(x)$ is Newton's identity relating the power sums $p_1, p_2$ to $e_1, e_2$.
$\square$

**Theorem 7.4 (Sub-subleading Laurent coefficient).** For normalized
$(f_i)_{i \in S}$ with $|S| = m$, writing $a_i$ and $b_i$ for the constant and
linear coefficients of $f_i$,
$$2\Big(\prod_{i \in S} f_i\Big)_{2-m}
= 2\sum_{i \in S} b_i + \Big(\sum_{i \in S} a_i\Big)^{2}
- \sum_{i \in S} a_i^{2},$$
equivalently
$$\Big(\prod_{i \in S} f_i\Big)_{2-m} = \sum_{i \in S} b_i
+ \sum_{i < j} a_i a_j .$$

*Proof sketch.* Coefficient transfer with $k = 2$, then Lemma 7.3 with
$g_i = U(f_i)$, using $(U(f_i))_1 = a_i$ and $(U(f_i))_2 = b_i$. $\square$

Theorems 7.2 and 7.4 are the first two levels of a hierarchy. At level $k$, the
coefficient at $q^{k-m}$ is a universal polynomial with rational coefficients in
the coefficients $a_i, b_i, \dots$ of the factors, and its shape is dictated by
the logarithm map: on the group $1 + q\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$ the formal logarithm
is an isomorphism onto $q\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$, converting the product $\prod_i
U(f_i)$ into the sum $\sum_i \log U(f_i)$; exponentiating back expresses the
level-$k$ coefficient as the degree-$k$ part of $\exp$ applied to a sum of power
sums, which is exactly the classical passage from power sums to elementary
symmetric functions. Levels $1$ and $2$ above are the visible face of this
mechanism; the general level is stated as Conjecture 9.1 below.

---

## 8. Specialization: the Monster

The Monster simple group $\mathbb{M}$ has order
$$|\mathbb{M}| = 808017424794512875886459904961710757005754368000000000$$
and exactly $194$ conjugacy classes. Monstrous Moonshine assigns to each class
$g$ the trace series $T_g = q^{-1} + \sum_{n\ge 1} c_g(n) q^n$, so that in our
notation $T_g = T[c_g]$ with $c_g(0) = 0$, and every $T_g$ is normalized (Lemma
2.9). Let
$$\Pi \;=\; \prod_{g} T_g$$
be the product over all $194$ classes.

**Theorem 8.1 (Monster-sized pole).** $\operatorname{ord}(\Pi) = -194$, and the
coefficient of $q^{-194}$ in $\Pi$ is $1$.

*Proof sketch.* Theorems 3.3 and 3.1 with $m = 194$. $\square$

**Theorem 8.2 (Not a power series).** $\Pi \notin \mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$.

*Proof sketch.* Theorem 3.5, since $194 \ge 1$. $\square$

**Theorem 8.3 (Unique correction and unit structure).** For $k \in
\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, $\operatorname{ord}(q^k \Pi) = 0$ iff $k = 194$; and
$q^{194}\Pi = \prod_g U(T_g)$ is a unit of $\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$ with constant
term $1$. Equivalently $\Pi = q^{-194}\prod_g U(T_g)$.

*Proof sketch.* Theorems 4.1, 4.4 and Corollary 5.2. $\square$

**Theorem 8.4 (Vanishing subleading coefficient).** Since $c_g(0) = 0$ for every
class $g$, the coefficient of $q^{-193}$ in $\Pi$ is $0$:
$$\Pi = q^{-194} + 0\cdot q^{-193} + \Big(\sum_{g} c_g(1)\Big) q^{-192} + \cdots.$$

*Proof sketch.* Theorem 7.2 gives the $q^{-193}$ coefficient as $\sum_g c_g(0) =
0$. Theorem 7.4 then gives $2 \cdot (\Pi)_{-192} = 2\sum_g c_g(1) + 0 - 0$, so
$(\Pi)_{-192} = \sum_g c_g(1)$. $\square$

The number $\sum_g c_g(1)$ is a pure character sum: $c_g(1)$ is the trace of $g$
on the graded piece $V^{\natural}_1$, which as a Monster representation is
$\mathbf{1} \oplus \mathbf{196883}$. So $\sum_g c_g(1) = \sum_g \big(1 +
\chi_{196883}(g)\big) = 194 + \sum_g \chi_{196883}(g)$, a sum over conjugacy
*classes* (not group elements) of the smallest faithful character of the Monster,
shifted by the number of classes.

**A verifiable two-factor instance.** Take the two classes $1A$ and $2A$, with
$$T_{1A} = J = q^{-1} + 196884\,q + 21493760\,q^2 + \cdots, \qquad
T_{2A} = q^{-1} + 4372\,q + 96256\,q^2 + \cdots .$$
Both have vanishing constant term. Theorem 3.3 gives
$\operatorname{ord}(J\cdot T_{2A}) = -2$ with leading coefficient $1$; Theorem
7.2 gives coefficient $0$ at $q^{-1}$; Theorem 7.4 gives the constant
coefficient
$$196884 + 4372 = 201256 .$$
So $J \cdot T_{2A} = q^{-2} + 0\cdot q^{-1} + 201256 + \cdots$. The numbers
$196884 = 196883 + 1$ and $4372 = 4371 + 1$ are the two observations that opened
moonshine; their sum appears here as a structural consequence of Newton's
identity at level $2$ rather than as a coincidence.

## 9. Discussion, applications and open problems

### 9.1 What the obstruction is good for

The practical content is a *design rule* for any construction in the moonshine
circle of ideas that multiplies trace functions. Suppose one builds an object
from $m$ hauptmoduln — for instance in twisted denominator identities for the
Monster Lie algebra, in replicability recursions relating $T_g(q)$ to
$T_{g^n}(q)$, in Hecke-type operators on the space of trace functions, or in
products indexed by subsets of conjugacy classes. Whatever the construction, the
result carries a pole of order exactly $m$, its leading coefficient is exactly
$1$, and if the target of the construction is required to be a hauptmodul (order
$-1$) or a holomorphic object (order $\ge 0$) then the construction is
*obliged* to correct by $q^{m}$ — and no other monomial will do (Theorem 4.1).
Because Theorem 4.4 says the corrected object is a unit, one may then invert it,
take its logarithm, or extract Newton-type invariants, all inside the group
$1 + q\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$.

Conversely, the obstruction is a quick falsifier. Any claimed identity asserting
that a product of $m \ge 2$ normalized series equals a normalized series, or a
power series, is false — regardless of the coefficients involved — because the
two sides sit in different fibres of a group homomorphism.

### 9.2 Scope and limitations

Three remarks delimit the result.

*The proof uses only that $\mathbb{C}$ is an integral domain.* Everything above
holds verbatim with $\mathbb{C}$ replaced by any integral domain $R$; over a ring
with zero divisors, Lemma 2.3 degrades to an inequality and the obstruction
becomes only a bound. The exactness of the pole order is precisely a
domain-theoretic phenomenon.

*The result is purely about the local behaviour at the cusp.* Nothing here uses
modularity, the invariance groups $\Gamma_0(n)+e,f,\dots$, or the genus-zero
property. It applies to any family of $q$-expansions with a simple monic pole,
which makes it robust but also means it cannot by itself distinguish moonshine
series from arbitrary series of the same shape. The strength of a purely
valuation-theoretic statement is exactly that it is insensitive to everything
else.

*The value group matters.* As stressed in §1.3, replacing $\mathbb{Z}\cup
\{\infty\}$ by $\mathbb{Z}$ with the convention $\operatorname{ord}(0) = 0$
makes the main theorem false for families that may contain $0$. The
$\mathbb{Z}$-valued statements in this paper are therefore always accompanied by
a non-vanishing hypothesis, which Corollary 3.2 supplies in the normalized case.

### 9.3 Conjecture: the Newton hierarchy at all levels

**Conjecture 9.1 (Newton hierarchy).** Let $f_i = q^{-1} + a_{i,0} + a_{i,1}q +
a_{i,2}q^2 + \cdots$, $i \in S$, $|S| = m$, be normalized. Then for every
$k \ge 0$ the Laurent coefficient of $\prod_i f_i$ at degree $k - m$ is a
universal polynomial with rational coefficients in the power sums
$p_r = \sum_i a_{i,n}$ — explicitly, the degree-$k$ part of
$\exp\!\big(\sum_{r \ge 1} (-1)^{r+1} p_r / r\big)$ applied to the logarithms of
the unit parts $U(f_i)$.

The key insight is that Corollary 5.2 reduces the question entirely to the
multiplicativity of $\prod_i U(f_i)$ inside $1 + q\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$, where the
formal logarithm is an isomorphism onto $q\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$, converting
products into sums of power sums. The conjecture is falsifiable in the strongest
sense: it predicts, for instance, the exact value of the constant coefficient in
the $m = 2$ case computed above, and a single mismatched truncated product would
refute it.

### 9.4 Conjecture: pole order detects the failure of the hauptmodul property

**Conjecture 9.2 (Pole order detects genus-zero failure).** Let $f$ be
normalized and let $H(f) \subseteq \mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)$ be the
$\mathbb{C}$-subalgebra generated by $f$ and $q$. Then $H(f)$ contains an element
of every integer order, the induced map $H(f)^{\times} \to \mathbb{Z}$ is
surjective, and its kernel is exactly the units of $H(f)$ lying in
$1 + q\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$. Consequently no finite product of normalized series
can be a hauptmodul unless $m = 1$.

The key insight is that Theorem 3.4 already shows normalized series are closed
under multiplication only in the trivial case, so the "hauptmodul property" is an
order-$(-1)$ condition and the obstruction is exactly the image of the order
homomorphism (Theorem 6.2).

### 9.5 Further directions

* **Higher-order poles.** Replace "simple monic pole" by "pole of order $d$ with
  leading coefficient $\lambda$". Orders still add, so a product of $m$ such
  series has order $-\sum_i d_i$ and leading coefficient $\prod_i \lambda_i$; the
  correction monomial is $q^{\sum_i d_i}$ and the corrected series is a unit iff
  every $\lambda_i \ne 0$. The results here are the case $d_i = 1$,
  $\lambda_i = 1$.
* **Several variables and higher-rank valuations.** For Hahn series with value
  group $\Gamma$ an arbitrary ordered abelian group, Lemmas 2.3–2.4 hold
  unchanged; the obstruction becomes membership in a coset of the subgroup
  generated by the individual orders. This is the natural home for multivariable
  moonshine-type products.
* **Effective coefficient bounds.** Combining the factorization of Corollary 5.2
  with growth estimates on the $c_g(n)$ should yield explicit asymptotics for the
  coefficients of $q^{194}\Pi$, i.e. for the character-sum data of the full
  moonshine product.
* **The subgroup generated by the normalized series.** Since $\mathcal{N}$
  generates, under multiplication and inversion, a subgroup of
  $\mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)^{\times}$ surjecting onto $\mathbb{Z}$ with kernel meeting
  $1 + q\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$, one may ask which unit power series arise as
  $\prod_i U(T_g)^{\pm 1}$ for moonshine data specifically — an arithmetic
  question about the multiplicative relations among McKay–Thompson series.

---

## 10. Conclusion

The class of normalized $q$-series — the shape shared by all $194$
McKay–Thompson series of the Monster — fails to be closed under multiplication,
and the failure is measured by a single integer, the pole order, with no slack
whatsoever. A product of $m$ such series has pole order exactly $m$ and leading
coefficient exactly $1$; it is normalized only when $m = 1$; it is never a power
series when $m \ge 1$; the unique monomial repairing it is $q^m$; and after the
repair the object is not merely regular but invertible. All of this flows from
one structural fact, the unique factorization of a normalized series as $q^{-1}$
times a principal unit power series, and from one structural reformulation, the
order as a surjective group homomorphism onto $\mathbb{Z}$ with disjoint fibres.
For the Monster the numbers are concrete and memorable: pole order $194$, unique
correction $q^{194}$, vanishing coefficient at $q^{-193}$, and character sum
$\sum_g c_g(1)$ at $q^{-192}$.

\begin{abstract}
A \emph{normalized} $q$-series is a formal Laurent series over $\CC$ of the shape
$f = q^{-1} + a_0 + a_1 q + a_2 q^2 + \cdots$: a simple pole of residue $1$ at
the cusp, followed by a power series. This is the shape of every McKay--Thompson
series of the Monster simple group. We prove that the class of normalized series
is \emph{not} closed under multiplication, and that the failure is measured
completely and sharply by a single integer. The order valuation on $\Cls$,
taking values in $\ZZ \cup \{\infty\}$, is additive on products; hence a product
of $m$ normalized series has order exactly $-m$ with leading coefficient exactly
$1$, so it is normalized if and only if $m = 1$, and for $m \ge 1$ it is not a
power series at all. The obstruction is removable in exactly one way: $q^{k}$
times the product has order $0$ if and only if $k = m$, and the corrected series
is then not merely a power series but a \emph{unit} of $\Cps$. The structural
reason is a unique factorization theorem --- every normalized series is uniquely
$q^{-1}$ times a power series with constant term $1$ --- together with the fact
that the order restricts to a surjective group homomorphism

coefficients past the pole, obtaining Newton-type identities in the elementary
symmetric functions of the factors' coefficients, and specialize to the $194$
conjugacy classes of the Monster: the full Monstrous Moonshine product has a pole
of order exactly $194$, its subleading coefficient vanishes under the standard
normalization, and its next coefficient is the character sum $\sum_g c_g(1)$.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Motivation}

Monstrous Moonshine attaches to each conjugacy class $g$ of the Monster simple
group $\mathbb{M}$ a \emph{McKay--Thompson series}
\[
  T_g(q) \;=\; \frac{1}{q} + \sum_{n \ge 1} c_g(n)\, q^{n},
\]
the graded trace of $g$ acting on the moonshine module $V^{\natural} =
\bigoplus_{n \ge -1} V^{\natural}_n$. There are exactly $194$ conjugacy classes
in $\mathbb{M}$, hence exactly $194$ such series. The class $1A$ gives the
normalized modular invariant $J = j - 744 = q^{-1} + 196884\,q + 21493760\,q^2 +
\cdots$, and the numerology $196884 = 196883 + 1$, $4372 = 4371 + 1$ opens the
subject.

The shared feature of all $194$ series is completely rigid: a simple pole with
residue $1$ at $q = 0$, and no deeper pole. This shape is what makes each $T_g$ a
\emph{hauptmodul} candidate for its invariance group. The question answered here
is the naive one that such a rigid shared shape provokes: is this class of series
stable under multiplication? Many constructions in and around moonshine ---
twisted denominator identities, replication formulas, Hecke-type operators,
products indexed by conjugacy classes --- combine several trace functions
multiplicatively, and it matters precisely what shape emerges. The answer is that
the class is stable only trivially, that the failure is governed by a single
integer, and that the integer determines its own repair.

\subsection{Summary of results}

Throughout, $\Cps$ denotes formal power series and $\Cls$ formal Laurent series
over $\CC$.

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Pole-Order Theorem} (Theorem~\ref{thm:pole}): a product of $m$
        normalized series has order exactly $-m$ and leading coefficient exactly
        $1$.
  \item \textbf{Non-closure} (Theorem~\ref{thm:nonclosure}): such a product is
        normalized iff $m = 1$; for $m \ge 1$ it is not a power series
        (Theorem~\ref{thm:genuinepole}).
  \item \textbf{Unique correction} (Theorem~\ref{thm:correction}): $q^k\prod_i
        f_i$ has order $0$ iff $k = m$.
  \item \textbf{Unit structure} (Theorem~\ref{thm:unit}): $q^m \prod_i f_i$ is a
        unit of $\Cps$ with constant term $1$.
  \item \textbf{Unique factorization} (Theorem~\ref{thm:factor}): every
        normalized $f$ is uniquely $q^{-1}u$ with $u \in \Cps$, $u(0) = 1$; hence
        $\prod_i f_i = q^{-m}\prod_i u_i$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:prodfactor}).
  \item \textbf{Valuation as a homomorphism} (Theorem~\ref{thm:hom}): the order
        induces a surjective group homomorphism $\Cls^{\times}\to\ZZ$, and the
        obstruction is membership in the fibre over $-m$
        (Corollary~\ref{cor:complete}).
  \item \textbf{Newton-type coefficient identities}
        (Theorems~\ref{thm:sub} and~\ref{thm:subsub}).
  \item \textbf{Monster specialization} (Section~\ref{sec:monster}): pole of
        order exactly $194$; unique correction $q^{194}$; vanishing coefficient
        at $q^{-193}$; coefficient $\sum_g c_g(1)$ at $q^{-192}$; and
        $J\cdot T_{2A} = q^{-2} + 0\cdot q^{-1} + 201256 + \cdots$.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{A boundary worth stating}\label{sec:boundary}

One design point is not cosmetic. It is standard to extend the order function to
the zero series; the two common conventions are $\ord(0) = \infty$ (values in
$\ZZ\cup\{\infty\}$, with $\infty$ absorbing) and $\ord(0) = 0$ (values in $\ZZ$,
so that the function is total). Only the first is compatible with unrestricted
additivity. With the second, ``a product of $m$ normalized series has order
$-m$'' is \emph{false} for families permitted to contain the zero series, and
false with no syntactic warning. Every general statement below therefore uses the
$\ZZ\cup\{\infty\}$-valued order; the $\ZZ$-valued versions carry an explicit
non-vanishing hypothesis.

\section{Setting and definitions}

\begin{definition}[Laurent series]
A \emph{formal Laurent series} over $\CC$ is a function $f\colon\ZZ\to\CC$,
written $f = \sum_{n\in\ZZ} f_n q^n$, whose support $\{n : f_n \ne 0\}$ is
bounded below. These form a field $\Cls$ under coefficientwise addition and the
convolution product $(fg)_n = \sum_{i+j=n} f_i g_j$, a finite sum by the support
condition. The subring of series supported in $\ZZ_{\ge 0}$ is the power series
ring $\Cps$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Order and leading coefficient]
For $f \ne 0$, the \emph{order} $\ord(f)\in\ZZ$ is $\min\{n : f_n \ne 0\}$ and
the \emph{leading coefficient} is $\lc(f) = f_{\ord(f)}$. We set
$\ord(0) = \infty$ in the ordered monoid $\ZZ\cup\{\infty\}$, where
$\infty + x = x + \infty = \infty$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Additivity]\label{lem:add}
For all $f,g\in\Cls$ we have $\ord(fg) = \ord(f) + \ord(g)$, and if
$f,g \ne 0$ then $\lc(fg) = \lc(f)\lc(g)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If either factor is $0$, both sides are $\infty$. Otherwise put $d = \ord f$,
$e = \ord g$. For $n < d+e$, every term $f_i g_j$ with $i+j=n$ has $i<d$ or
$j<e$, hence vanishes; for $n = d+e$ the only surviving term is $f_d g_e$, which
is nonzero because $\CC$ is an integral domain.
\end{proof}

Additivity is the only nontrivial input to this paper; that it is an
\emph{equality} rather than an inequality --- a consequence of $\CC$ being a
domain --- is what turns every bound below into an exact obstruction.

\begin{lemma}[Finite products]\label{lem:prodadd}
For any finite index set $S$ and family $(f_i)_{i\in S}$ in $\Cls$,
\[
  \ord\Big(\prod_{i\in S} f_i\Big) \;=\; \sum_{i\in S}\ord(f_i)
  \qquad\text{in }\ZZ\cup\{\infty\}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $|S|$ using Lemma~\ref{lem:add}; the empty product is $1$, of order
$0$. No non-vanishing hypothesis is needed, since $\infty$ absorbs.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Units of $\Cps$]\label{lem:units}
A power series $u$ is invertible in $\Cps$ if and only if $u_0 \ne 0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Necessity is clear from $u_0v_0 = 1$. For sufficiency solve
$\sum_{i+j=n}u_iv_j = \delta_{n,0}$ recursively: $v_0 = u_0^{-1}$ and
$v_n = -u_0^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_i v_{n-i}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Normalized series]\label{def:norm}
A Laurent series $f$ is \emph{normalized} if $f_{-1} = 1$ and $f_n = 0$ for all
$n < -1$; equivalently $f = q^{-1} + a_0 + a_1 q + a_2 q^2 + \cdots$. Write
$\Norm \subset \Cls$ for the set of normalized series.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:normbasic}
If $f$ is normalized then $f \ne 0$, $\ord(f) = -1$ and $\lc(f) = 1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$f_{-1} = 1 \ne 0$ shows $f \ne 0$ and that $-1$ is in the support; the second
condition says nothing below $-1$ is in the support, so $-1$ is its minimum, and
$\lc(f) = f_{-1} = 1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Trace-series model]\label{def:trace}
For a sequence $c\colon\ZZ_{\ge0}\to\CC$ put
$T[c] = q^{-1} + \sum_{n\ge0} c(n)q^{n}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:tracenorm}
$T[c]$ is normalized for every $c$, with $T[c]_0 = c(0)$ and $T[c]_1 = c(1)$.
\end{lemma}

Every McKay--Thompson series is of the form $T[c]$ with $c(0) = 0$.

\section{The pole-order theorem}

Fix a finite index set $S$ with $|S| = m$ and a family $(f_i)_{i\in S}$ of
normalized series; write $P = \prod_{i\in S} f_i$.

\begin{theorem}[Leading coefficient]\label{thm:lc}
$\lc(P) = 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $|S|$ using multiplicativity of $\lc$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:add}) and
$\lc(f_i) = 1$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:normbasic}); the empty product has leading
coefficient $1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:nonzero}
$P \ne 0$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If $P = 0$ then $P$ has no nonzero coefficient at all, contradicting
Theorem~\ref{thm:lc}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Pole-Order Theorem]\label{thm:pole}
$\ord\big(\prod_{i\in S} f_i\big) = -m$ where $m = |S|$; equivalently
$P = q^{-m} + (\text{higher order terms})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:prodadd} the order of $P$ is $\sum_{i\in S}\ord(f_i) =
\sum_{i\in S}(-1) = -m$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:normbasic}.
Corollary~\ref{cor:nonzero} guarantees the value is finite, so the statement is
meaningful as an equality of integers. With Theorem~\ref{thm:lc}, the expansion
begins with $1\cdot q^{-m}$.
\end{proof}

The content of Theorem~\ref{thm:pole} is the word \emph{exactly}: no cancellation
is possible. Poles of normalized series add with perfect fidelity because the
leading coefficients are all $1$ and $\CC$ is a domain.

\begin{theorem}[Non-closure]\label{thm:nonclosure}
$P$ is normalized if and only if $m = 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If $P$ is normalized then $\ord(P) = -1$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:normbasic}, while
$\ord(P) = -m$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:pole}; hence $m = 1$. Conversely if $m=1$ then
$P = f_i$ for the unique $i\in S$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Genuine pole]\label{thm:genuinepole}
If $m \ge 1$ then $P\notin\Cps$: it is not the image of any formal power series.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Theorems~\ref{thm:lc} and~\ref{thm:pole} the coefficient of $q^{-m}$ in $P$
is $1$, while every element of $\Cps$ has vanishing coefficients in all negative
degrees, and $-m < 0$.
\end{proof}

\section{Correcting the pole, and the uniqueness of the correction}

\begin{theorem}[Unique monomial correction]\label{thm:correction}
For $k\in\ZZ_{\ge0}$ we have $\ord\big(q^{k}\prod_{i\in S}f_i\big) = 0$ if and
only if $k = m$. In particular $\ord\big(q^{m}\prod_i f_i\big) = 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\ord(q^k) = k$, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:prodadd} and Theorem~\ref{thm:pole} the
order of the corrected product is $k - m$, which vanishes iff $k = m$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Leading coefficient survives]\label{thm:lcsurvive}
$\lc\big(q^m\prod_i f_i\big) = 1$; equivalently the constant term of the
corrected series is $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Multiplicativity of $\lc$ with $\lc(q^m) = 1$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:lc}. Since the
order is $0$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:correction}, the leading coefficient is the
constant term.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Unit part]\label{def:unitpart}
For normalized $f$ define $U(f)\in\Cps$ by $U(f)_n = f_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 0$. Then
$U(f) = qf$ as Laurent series, $U(f)_0 = f_{-1} = 1$, $U(f)_1 = f_0$ and
$U(f)_2 = f_1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Unit structure of the corrected product]\label{thm:unit}
For normalized $(f_i)_{i\in S}$,
\[
  q^{m}\prod_{i\in S} f_i \;=\; \prod_{i\in S} U(f_i) \quad\text{in }\Cps,
\]
and this power series is a \emph{unit} of $\Cps$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Each $U(f_i) = qf_i$, so $\prod_i U(f_i) = q^m\prod_i f_i$. Each $U(f_i)$ has
constant term $1$, hence is a unit by Lemma~\ref{lem:units}; a finite product of
units is a unit.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:unit} upgrades Theorem~\ref{thm:correction} from a numerical
statement (``the order is $0$'') to a structural one: after correction the
product lands not merely in the ring $\Cps$ but in the group $\Cps^{\times}$,
indeed in the subgroup $1 + q\Cps$ of principal units.

\section{Unique factorization of normalized series}

\begin{theorem}[Structure theorem]\label{thm:factor}
For each normalized $f$ there is a \emph{unique} power series $u$ with constant
term $1$ such that $f = q^{-1}u$, namely $u = U(f)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Existence: $q^{-1}U(f) = q^{-1}(qf) = f$ and $U(f)_0 = f_{-1} = 1$. Uniqueness:
if $f = q^{-1}v$ with $v\in\Cps$, multiplying by the field unit $q$ gives
$v = qf = U(f)$, and $\Cps\hookrightarrow\Cls$ is injective.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Factorization of the product]\label{cor:prodfactor}
For normalized $(f_i)_{i\in S}$ with $|S| = m$,
\[
  \prod_{i\in S} f_i \;=\; q^{-m}\cdot\prod_{i\in S} U(f_i),
\]
a monomial of degree $-m$ times a unit of $\Cps$ with constant term $1$.
\end{corollary}

Corollary~\ref{cor:prodfactor} is the conceptual root of the paper. Once one
knows that the normalized series are exactly the elements $q^{-1}u$ with
$u \in 1 + q\Cps$, everything else is bookkeeping in the decomposition
\[
  \Cls^{\times} \;\cong\; q^{\ZZ}\times\CC^{\times}\times\big(1 + q\Cps\big),
\]
under which $\Norm$ is the slice $\{q^{-1}\}\times\{1\}\times(1 + q\Cps)$.
Multiplying $m$ elements of the slice multiplies the monomial components, sending
$q^{-1}\mapsto q^{-m}$; the slice is closed under multiplication only when
$m=1$, because $\{-1\}$ is closed under addition in $\ZZ$ only for one-fold sums.

\section{The valuation as a group homomorphism}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:ordmul}
For nonzero $x,y\in\Cls$, $\ord(xy) = \ord(x)+\ord(y)$ in $\ZZ$, and
$\ord(1) = 0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Order homomorphism]\label{thm:hom}
The map $\ord\colon\Cls^{\times}\to\ZZ$ is a surjective group homomorphism from
the multiplicative group of the field of Laurent series onto the additive group
of integers.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Homomorphism: Lemma~\ref{lem:ordmul}, noting that every nonzero element of a
field is a unit. Surjectivity: $q^{k}$ is invertible with inverse $q^{-k}$ and
$\ord(q^{k}) = k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:normfibre}
Every normalized series is a unit of $\Cls$ and lies in the fibre
$\ord^{-1}(-1)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{corollary}[Completeness of the obstruction]\label{cor:complete}
A product of $m$ normalized series lies in the fibre $\ord^{-1}(-m)$ and --- the
fibres of a homomorphism being pairwise disjoint --- in no other fibre. In
particular it lies in $\ord^{-1}(-1)$ iff $m = 1$.
\end{corollary}

This is the sense in which the pole order is a \emph{complete} obstruction rather
than a necessary condition: it is the value of a homomorphism, and homomorphism
values partition the group. The kernel $\ord^{-1}(0) = \Cps^{\times}$ is exactly
the group of unit power series, so Corollary~\ref{cor:prodfactor} exhibits the
standard splitting: every nonzero Laurent series is uniquely a monomial times an
element of the kernel.

\section{Newton-type identities past the pole}

Corollary~\ref{cor:prodfactor} transfers coefficient questions about
$\prod_i f_i$ to coefficient questions about a product of power series with
constant term $1$: for $k\ge0$,
\[
  \Big(\prod_{i\in S} f_i\Big)_{k-m} \;=\; \Big(\prod_{i\in S} U(f_i)\Big)_{k}.
\]
Write $f_i = q^{-1} + a_i + b_i q + \cdots$, so $U(f_i) = 1 + a_i q + b_i q^2 +
\cdots$.

\begin{lemma}[Level 1]\label{lem:lev1}
If $(g_i)_{i\in S}$ are power series with $(g_i)_0 = 1$ then
$\big(\prod_{i\in S} g_i\big)_1 = \sum_{i\in S}(g_i)_1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $|S|$ using $(gh)_1 = g_0h_1 + g_1h_0$ and the fact that a product
of series with constant term $1$ again has constant term $1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Subleading Laurent coefficient]\label{thm:sub}
For normalized $(f_i)_{i\in S}$ with $|S| = m$,
\[
  \Big(\prod_{i\in S} f_i\Big)_{1-m} \;=\; \sum_{i\in S} a_i,
\]
the sum of the constant terms of the factors.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Coefficient transfer with $k=1$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:lev1} applied to
$g_i = U(f_i)$, noting $(U(f_i))_1 = a_i$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Level 2]\label{lem:lev2}
If $(g_i)_{i\in S}$ are power series with $(g_i)_0 = 1$ then
\[
  2\Big(\prod_{i\in S} g_i\Big)_2
  \;=\; 2\sum_{i\in S}(g_i)_2 + \Big(\sum_{i\in S}(g_i)_1\Big)^{2}
  - \sum_{i\in S}(g_i)_1^{2}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $|S|$. The inductive step uses $(gh)_2 = g_0h_2 + g_1h_1 + g_2h_0$
with $g_0 = h_0 = 1$, the level-$1$ identity for the partial product, and the
algebraic identity $(A+x)^2 - (A^2+x^2) = 2Ax$. The denominator-free form avoids
dividing by $2$; equivalently $\big(\prod g_i\big)_2 = \sum_i (g_i)_2 +
e_2\big((g_i)_1\big)$, since $\big(\sum x_i\big)^2 - \sum x_i^2 = 2e_2(x)$ is
Newton's identity relating the power sums $p_1,p_2$ to $e_1,e_2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sub-subleading Laurent coefficient]\label{thm:subsub}
For normalized $(f_i)_{i\in S}$ with $|S| = m$, writing $a_i$ and $b_i$ for the
constant and linear coefficients of $f_i$,
\[
  2\Big(\prod_{i\in S} f_i\Big)_{2-m}
  \;=\; 2\sum_{i\in S} b_i + \Big(\sum_{i\in S} a_i\Big)^{2}
  - \sum_{i\in S} a_i^{2},
\]
equivalently $\big(\prod_{i} f_i\big)_{2-m} = \sum_i b_i + \sum_{i<j} a_ia_j$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Coefficient transfer with $k=2$, then Lemma~\ref{lem:lev2} applied to
$g_i = U(f_i)$, using $(U(f_i))_1 = a_i$ and $(U(f_i))_2 = b_i$.
\end{proof}

Theorems~\ref{thm:sub} and~\ref{thm:subsub} are the first two levels of a
hierarchy. At level $k$ the coefficient at $q^{k-m}$ is a universal polynomial
with rational coefficients in the coefficients of the factors, whose shape is
dictated by the formal logarithm: on $1 + q\Cps$ it is an isomorphism onto
$q\Cps$, converting $\prod_i U(f_i)$ into $\sum_i \log U(f_i)$, and
exponentiating back expresses the level-$k$ coefficient as the degree-$k$ part of
$\exp$ applied to a sum of power sums --- the classical passage from power sums
to elementary symmetric functions.

\section{Specialization: the Monster}\label{sec:monster}

The Monster simple group $\mathbb{M}$ has order
\[
  |\mathbb{M}| = 808017424794512875886459904961710757005754368000000000
\]
and exactly $194$ conjugacy classes. Monstrous Moonshine assigns to each class
$g$ the series $T_g = q^{-1} + \sum_{n\ge1}c_g(n)q^{n}$, so $T_g = T[c_g]$ with
$c_g(0) = 0$ and each $T_g$ is normalized (Lemma~\ref{lem:tracenorm}). Let
$\Pi = \prod_g T_g$ be the product over all $194$ classes.

\begin{theorem}[Monster-sized pole]\label{thm:monsterpole}
$\ord(\Pi) = -194$, and the coefficient of $q^{-194}$ in $\Pi$ is $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Theorems~\ref{thm:pole} and~\ref{thm:lc} with $m = 194$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Not a power series]
$\Pi\notin\Cps$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Theorem~\ref{thm:genuinepole}, since $194 \ge 1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Unique correction and unit structure]
For $k\in\ZZ_{\ge0}$, $\ord(q^{k}\Pi) = 0$ iff $k = 194$; and
$q^{194}\Pi = \prod_g U(T_g)$ is a unit of $\Cps$ with constant term $1$.
Equivalently $\Pi = q^{-194}\prod_g U(T_g)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Theorems~\ref{thm:correction} and~\ref{thm:unit}, and
Corollary~\ref{cor:prodfactor}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Vanishing subleading coefficient]\label{thm:monstersub}
Since $c_g(0) = 0$ for every class $g$,
\[
  \Pi \;=\; q^{-194} \;+\; 0\cdot q^{-193} \;+\;
  \Big(\sum_g c_g(1)\Big) q^{-192} \;+\; \cdots.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Theorem~\ref{thm:sub} gives the $q^{-193}$ coefficient as $\sum_g c_g(0) = 0$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:subsub} then gives $2(\Pi)_{-192} = 2\sum_g c_g(1) + 0 - 0$.
\end{proof}

The quantity $\sum_g c_g(1)$ is a pure character sum: $c_g(1)$ is the trace of
$g$ on $V^{\natural}_1 \cong \mathbf{1}\oplus\mathbf{196883}$, so
$\sum_g c_g(1) = 194 + \sum_g \chi_{196883}(g)$, the sum over conjugacy classes
of the smallest faithful character of the Monster, shifted by the number of
classes.

\begin{example}[A verifiable two-factor instance]
Take the classes $1A$ and $2A$, with
\[
  T_{1A} = J = q^{-1} + 196884\,q + 21493760\,q^2 + \cdots, \qquad
  T_{2A} = q^{-1} + 4372\,q + 96256\,q^2 + \cdots,
\]
both with vanishing constant term. Theorem~\ref{thm:pole} gives
$\ord(J\cdot T_{2A}) = -2$ with leading coefficient $1$;
Theorem~\ref{thm:sub} gives coefficient $0$ at $q^{-1}$; and
Theorem~\ref{thm:subsub} gives the constant coefficient $196884 + 4372 =
201256$. Thus $J\cdot T_{2A} = q^{-2} + 0\cdot q^{-1} + 201256 + \cdots$. The
numbers $196884 = 196883+1$ and $4372 = 4371+1$ are the two observations that
opened moonshine; their sum appears here as a structural consequence of Newton's
identity at level $2$.
\end{example}

\section{Discussion and open problems}

\subsection{What the obstruction is good for}

The practical content is a design rule for any construction that multiplies trace
functions --- twisted denominator identities for the Monster Lie algebra,
replicability recursions relating $T_g(q)$ to $T_{g^n}(q)$, Hecke-type operators,
or products indexed by subsets of conjugacy classes. Whatever the construction,
the result carries a pole of order exactly $m$ with leading coefficient exactly
$1$; if the target is required to be a hauptmodul (order $-1$) or holomorphic
(order $\ge 0$), the construction is \emph{obliged} to correct by $q^{m}$, and no
other monomial will do (Theorem~\ref{thm:correction}). Because
Theorem~\ref{thm:unit} makes the corrected object a unit, one may then invert it,
take its logarithm, or extract Newton-type invariants inside the group
$1 + q\Cps$. Conversely the obstruction is a quick falsifier: any claimed
identity asserting that a product of $m\ge2$ normalized series is normalized, or
is a power series, is false regardless of the coefficients involved, because the
two sides lie in different fibres of a group homomorphism.

\subsection{Scope and limitations}

Three remarks delimit the result. First, the proofs use only that $\CC$ is an
integral domain: everything holds over any integral domain, while over a ring
with zero divisors Lemma~\ref{lem:add} degrades to an inequality and the
obstruction becomes a bound rather than an equality. Second, the result is purely
local at the cusp; it uses no modularity, no invariance groups, and no genus-zero
property, which makes it robust but means it cannot by itself distinguish
moonshine series from arbitrary series of the same shape. Third, as stressed in
Section~\ref{sec:boundary}, the value group matters: replacing $\ZZ\cup\{\infty\}$
by $\ZZ$ with $\ord(0) = 0$ makes the main theorem false for families that may
contain $0$.

\subsection{Conjectures}

\begin{conjecture}[Newton hierarchy at all levels]
Let $f_i = q^{-1} + a_{i,0} + a_{i,1}q + a_{i,2}q^2 + \cdots$, $i\in S$,
$|S| = m$, be normalized. Then for every $k \ge 0$ the Laurent coefficient of
$\prod_i f_i$ at degree $k-m$ is a universal polynomial with rational
coefficients in the power sums $p_r = \sum_i a_{i,n}$ --- explicitly, the
degree-$k$ part of $\exp\big(\sum_{r\ge1}(-1)^{r+1}p_r/r\big)$ applied to the
logarithms of the unit parts $U(f_i)$.
\end{conjecture}

The key insight is that Corollary~\ref{cor:prodfactor} reduces the question to
the multiplicativity of $\prod_i U(f_i)$ inside $1 + q\Cps$, where the formal
logarithm is an isomorphism onto $q\Cps$, converting products into sums of power
sums. The conjecture is falsifiable in the strongest sense: it predicts the exact
constant coefficient in the $m = 2$ case computed above, and a single mismatched
truncated product would refute it.

\begin{conjecture}[Pole order detects genus-zero failure]
Let $f$ be normalized and let $H(f)\subseteq\Cls$ be the $\CC$-subalgebra
generated by $f$ and $q$. Then $H(f)$ contains an element of every integer order,
the induced map $H(f)^{\times}\to\ZZ$ is surjective, and its kernel is exactly the
units of $H(f)$ lying in $1 + q\Cps$. Consequently no finite product of
normalized series can be a hauptmodul unless $m = 1$.
\end{conjecture}

The key insight is that Theorem~\ref{thm:nonclosure} already shows normalized
series are closed under multiplication only in the trivial case, so the
hauptmodul property is an order-$(-1)$ condition and the obstruction is exactly
the image of the order homomorphism (Theorem~\ref{thm:hom}).

\subsection{Further directions}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Higher-order poles.} Replace ``simple monic pole'' by ``pole of
        order $d_i$ with leading coefficient $\lambda_i$''. Orders still add, so
        the product has order $-\sum_i d_i$ and leading coefficient
        $\prod_i\lambda_i$; the correction monomial is $q^{\sum_i d_i}$ and the
        corrected series is a unit iff every $\lambda_i \ne 0$.
  \item \textbf{Several variables, higher-rank valuations.} For Hahn series with
        value group an arbitrary ordered abelian group, Lemmas~\ref{lem:add}
        and~\ref{lem:prodadd} hold unchanged; the obstruction becomes membership
        in a coset of the subgroup generated by the individual orders.
  \item \textbf{Effective coefficient bounds.} Combining
        Corollary~\ref{cor:prodfactor} with growth estimates on the $c_g(n)$
        should yield explicit asymptotics for the coefficients of $q^{194}\Pi$.
  \item \textbf{The subgroup generated by the normalized series.} Which unit
        power series arise as $\prod_i U(T_g)^{\pm1}$ for moonshine data
        specifically? This is an arithmetic question about multiplicative
        relations among McKay--Thompson series.
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}

The class of normalized $q$-series --- the shape shared by all $194$
McKay--Thompson series of the Monster --- fails to be closed under
multiplication, and the failure is measured by a single integer, the pole order,
with no slack whatsoever. A product of $m$ such series has pole order exactly $m$
and leading coefficient exactly $1$; it is normalized only when $m = 1$; it is
never a power series when $m \ge 1$; the unique monomial repairing it is $q^{m}$;
and after the repair the object is not merely regular but invertible. All of this
flows from the unique factorization of a normalized series as $q^{-1}$ times a
principal unit power series, and from the reformulation of the order as a
surjective group homomorphism onto $\ZZ$ with disjoint fibres. For the Monster
the numbers are concrete: pole order $194$, unique correction $q^{194}$,
vanishing coefficient at $q^{-193}$, and character sum $\sum_g c_g(1)$ at
$q^{-192}$.

Scalar = Fraction

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Truncated Laurent series
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


class Laurent:
    """A formal Laurent series truncated to a finite window of exponents.

    The series is stored as a starting exponent ``val`` together with a list of
    coefficients, ``coeffs[j]`` being the coefficient of ``q**(val + j)``.  The
    window is *exact*: every coefficient in degrees ``val .. val+len-1`` is
    correct, and nothing is claimed beyond.
    """

    __slots__ = ("val", "coeffs")

    def __init__(self, val: int, coeffs: Sequence[Scalar]) -> None:
        self.val: int = val
        self.coeffs: List[Scalar] = [Fraction(c) for c in coeffs]

    # -- basic accessors ----------------------------------------------------

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return len(self.coeffs)

    def coeff(self, n: int) -> Scalar:
        """Coefficient of ``q**n`` (zero outside the stored window)."""
        j = n - self.val
        if 0 <= j < len(self.coeffs):
            return self.coeffs[j]
        return Fraction(0)

    def order(self) -> float | int:
        """Smallest exponent with nonzero coefficient; ``inf`` if all vanish.

        Returning ``math.inf`` for the zero series mirrors the convention that
        the order takes values in Z u {infinity}, with infinity absorbing under
        addition.  This convention is *required* for unrestricted additivity.
        """
        for j, c in enumerate(self.coeffs):
            if c != 0:
                return self.val + j
        return float("inf")

    def leading_coeff(self) -> Scalar:
        for c in self.coeffs:
            if c != 0:
                return c
        return Fraction(0)

    # -- ring operations ----------------------------------------------------

    def __mul__(self, other: "Laurent") -> "Laurent":
        n = min(len(self), len(other))
        out: List[Scalar] = [Fraction(0)] * n
        for i, a in enumerate(self.coeffs):
            if a == 0 or i >= n:
                continue
            for j, b in enumerate(other.coeffs):
                if i + j >= n:
                    break
                out[i + j] += a * b
        return Laurent(self.val + other.val, out)

    def shift(self, k: int) -> "Laurent":
        """Multiply by ``q**k``."""
        return Laurent(self.val + k, list(self.coeffs))

    def truncate(self, n: int) -> "Laurent":
        return Laurent(self.val, self.coeffs[:n])

    # -- display ------------------------------------------------------------

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        parts: List[str] = []
        for j, c in enumerate(self.coeffs):
            if c == 0:
                continue
            e = self.val + j
            cs = str(c) if c.denominator != 1 else str(c.numerator)
            if e == 0:
                parts.append(cs)
            elif e == 1:
                parts.append(f"{cs}*q")
            else:
                parts.append(f"{cs}*q^{e}")
        return " + ".join(parts) + " + ..." if parts else "0"


def one(width: int = 8) -> Laurent:
    return Laurent(0, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (width - 1))


def q_pow(k: int, width: int = 8) -> Laurent:
    return Laurent(k, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (width - 1))


def product(series: Iterable[Laurent], width: int = 8) -> Laurent:
    acc = one(width)
    for f in series:
        acc = acc * f
    return acc


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Normalized series and their unit parts
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def normalized(tail: Sequence[Scalar]) -> Laurent:
    """Build ``q^{-1} + tail[0] + tail[1] q + tail[2] q^2 + ...``."""
    return Laurent(-1, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(t) for t in tail])


def is_normalized(f: Laurent) -> bool:
    """Coefficient at -1 equals 1 and everything below -1 vanishes."""
    if f.coeff(-1) != 1:
        return False
    return all(f.coeff(n) == 0 for n in range(f.val, -1))


def unit_part(f: Laurent) -> Laurent:
    """``U(f) = q * f``: a power series with constant term 1 when f is normalized."""
    return f.shift(1)


def invert_unit(u: Laurent) -> Laurent:
    """Inverse of a power series with nonzero constant term (recursive solve)."""
    assert u.val == 0 and u.coeff(0) != 0, "not a unit of C[[q]]"
    n = len(u)
    v: List[Scalar] = [Fraction(0)] * n
    v[0] = 1 / u.coeff(0)
    for k in range(1, n):
        s = sum(u.coeff(i) * v[k - i] for i in range(1, k + 1))
        v[k] = -s / u.coeff(0)
    return Laurent(0, v)

    "2A": (4372, 96256),

MONSTER_CLASS_COUNT: int = 194


def moonshine_like_family(rng: random.Random, count: int, width: int = 8) -> List[Laurent]:
    """A family of ``count`` normalized series with vanishing constant terms.

    The first two entries carry the genuine coefficients of the McKay-Thompson
    series for the classes 1A and 2A; the remaining entries are illustrative
    stand-ins with the same shape (constant term 0), which is all the theorems
    below depend on.
    """
    family: List[Laurent] = []
    for name in ("1A", "2A"):
        c1, c2 = MOONSHINE_DATA[name]
        family.append(normalized([0, c1, c2] + [0] * (width - 4)))
    while len(family) < count:
        family.append(normalized([0] + [rng.randint(-10**4, 10**5) for _ in range(width - 2)]))
    return family[:count]


def demo_monster(seed: int = 194) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("6.  THE MONSTER  --  194 conjugacy classes, pole of order exactly 194")
    print("=" * 74)

    print(f"  sum of linear coefficients    = {char_sum}   (must agree)")
    print(f"  agreement                     = {P.coeff(2 - m) == char_sum}")

    print("\n  Unique correction: ord(q^k * prod) = 0 only for k = 194.")
    for k in (192, 193, 194, 195):

    U = q_pow(m, width=8) * P
    print(f"\n  q^194 * prod has constant term {U.coeff(0)} -> a unit of C[[q]].")
    print(f"  The product is NOT a power series: its coefficient at q^-194 is "

        addition.  This convention is *required* for unrestricted additivity.

    def leading_coeff(self) -> Scalar:

            if c != 0:

        return Fraction(0)

    def shift(self, k: int) -> "Laurent":
        """Multiply by ``q**k``."""
        return Laurent(self.val + k, list(self.coeffs))

    def truncate(self, n: int) -> "Laurent":
        return Laurent(self.val, self.coeffs[:n])

    # -- display ------------------------------------------------------------

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        parts: List[str] = []
        for j, c in enumerate(self.coeffs):
            if c == 0:
                continue
            e = self.val + j
            cs = str(c) if c.denominator != 1 else str(c.numerator)
            if e == 0:
                parts.append(cs)
            elif e == 1:
                parts.append(f"{cs}*q")
            else:
                parts.append(f"{cs}*q^{e}")
        return " + ".join(parts) + " + ..." if parts else "0"


def one(width: int = 8) -> Laurent:
    return Laurent(0, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (width - 1))


def q_pow(k: int, width: int = 8) -> Laurent:
    return Laurent(k, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (width - 1))


def product(series: Iterable[Laurent], width: int = 8) -> Laurent:
    acc = one(width)
    for f in series:
        acc = acc * f
    return acc


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Normalized series and their unit parts
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def normalized(tail: Sequence[Scalar]) -> Laurent:
    """Build ``q^{-1} + tail[0] + tail[1] q + tail[2] q^2 + ...``."""
    return Laurent(-1, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(t) for t in tail])


def is_normalized(f: Laurent) -> bool:
    """Coefficient at -1 equals 1 and everything below -1 vanishes."""
    if f.coeff(-1) != 1:
        return False
    return all(f.coeff(n) == 0 for n in range(f.val, -1))


def unit_part(f: Laurent) -> Laurent:
    """``U(f) = q * f``: a power series with constant term 1 when f is normalized."""
    return f.shift(1)


def invert_unit(u: Laurent) -> Laurent:
    """Inverse of a power series with nonzero constant term (recursive solve)."""
    assert u.val == 0 and u.coeff(0) != 0, "not a unit of C[[q]]"
    n = len(u)
    v: List[Scalar] = [Fraction(0)] * n
    v[0] = 1 / u.coeff(0)
    for k in range(1, n):
        s = sum(u.coeff(i) * v[k - i] for i in range(1, k + 1))
        v[k] = -s / u.coeff(0)
    return Laurent(0, v)

def moonshine_like_family(rng: random.Random, count: int, width: int = 8) -> List[Laurent]:
    """A family of ``count`` normalized series with vanishing constant terms.

    The first two entries carry the genuine coefficients of the McKay-Thompson
    series for the classes 1A and 2A; the remaining entries are illustrative
    stand-ins with the same shape (constant term 0), which is all the theorems

    family: List[Laurent] = []
    for name in ("1A", "2A"):
        c1, c2 = MOONSHINE_DATA[name]

    while len(family) < count:
        family.append(normalized([0] + [rng.randint(-10**4, 10**5) for _ in range(width - 2)]))
    return family[:count]

from typing import List, Sequence

N = 8  # number of power-series coefficients tracked


def ps_mul(a: Sequence[Fraction], b: Sequence[Fraction]) -> List[Fraction]:
    out = [Fraction(0)] * N
    for i in range(N):
        if a[i] == 0:
            continue
        for j in range(N - i):
            out[i + j] += a[i] * b[j]
    return out


def ps_log(u: Sequence[Fraction]) -> List[Fraction]:
    """log(u) for u = 1 + O(q), via log(1+x) = x - x^2/2 + x^3/3 - ..."""
    assert u[0] == 1
    x = [Fraction(0)] + list(u[1:])
    term = [Fraction(0)] * N
    term[0] = Fraction(1)
    acc = [Fraction(0)] * N
    power = [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (N - 1)
    for r in range(1, N):
        power = ps_mul(power, x)
        sign = Fraction((-1) ** (r + 1), r)
        for i in range(N):
            acc[i] += sign * power[i]
    return acc


def ps_exp(v: Sequence[Fraction]) -> List[Fraction]:
    """exp(v) for v = O(q), via the exponential series."""
    assert v[0] == 0
    acc = [Fraction(0)] * N
    acc[0] = Fraction(1)
    power = [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (N - 1)
    fact = Fraction(1)
    for r in range(1, N):
        power = ps_mul(power, v)
        fact *= r
        for i in range(N):
            acc[i] += power[i] / fact
    return acc


def unit_part(tail: Sequence[int]) -> List[Fraction]:
    """U(f) = q*f = 1 + a q + b q^2 + ... for f = q^{-1} + a + b q + ..."""
    return [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(t) for t in tail[: N - 1]] + \
           [Fraction(0)] * max(0, N - 1 - len(tail))

    print("Product of m =", m, "normalized series -> pole of order", -m)

    b = [Fraction(f[1]) for f in factors]

    print("\nThe log/exp route is the mechanism behind every level: products of")
    print("principal units become sums of logarithms, and sums of logarithms")
    print("are power sums, which exponentiate to elementary symmetric functions.")

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple, Union

Scalar = Fraction
Series = Tuple[int, List[Scalar]]  # (starting exponent v, coeffs of q^v, q^{v+1}, ...)


def make_series(val: int, coeffs: Sequence[Union[int, Fraction]]) -> Series:
    """Normalize user input into an exact rational coefficient window."""
    return (val, [Fraction(c) for c in coeffs])


def mul(f: Series, g: Series) -> Series:
    """Cauchy product, truncated to the shorter of the two windows.

    Complexity: O(n^2) coefficient multiplications for windows of length n.
    """
    (vf, cf), (vg, cg) = f, g
    n = min(len(cf), len(cg))
    out: List[Scalar] = [Fraction(0)] * n
    for i, a in enumerate(cf[:n]):
        if a == 0:
            continue
        for j, b in enumerate(cg[: n - i]):
            out[i + j] += a * b
    return (vf + vg, out)


def order(f: Series) -> Union[int, float]:
    """Order valuation with values in Z u {infinity}; infinity for the zero series.

    The infinite value is essential: it is the unique convention making the
    order additive on all products without a non-vanishing hypothesis.
    """
    v, c = f
    for j, a in enumerate(c):
        if a != 0:
            return v + j
    return float("inf")


def leading_coeff(f: Series) -> Scalar:
    for a in f[1]:
        if a != 0:
            return a
    return Fraction(0)


def prod(series: Sequence[Series], window: int) -> Series:
    """Product of a finite family, evaluated on a window of the given length.

    Complexity: O(m * window^2) for m factors.
    """
    acc: Series = (0, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (window - 1))
    for f in series:
        acc = mul(acc, f)
    return acc


def order_of_product(series: Sequence[Series], window: int) -> Union[int, float]:

    Direct evaluation multiplies everything out; the valuation-theoretic route

Scalar = Fraction
Series = Tuple[int, List[Scalar]]


def normalized(tail: Sequence[int | Fraction]) -> Series:

    return (-1, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(t) for t in tail])

    (vf, cf), (vg, cg) = f, g
    n = min(len(cf), len(cg))

    for i, a in enumerate(cf[:n]):

    """Multiply by q^k: shift the starting exponent."""
    return (f[0] + k, list(f[1]))

    return float("inf")

    """U(f) = q*f, a power series of constant term 1 when f is normalized."""
    return shift(f, 1)

    """Inverse of a power series with constant term 1.

    v[0] = Fraction(1)

  input[type=number]{width:110px;padding:4px 6px;border:1px solid var(--line);
                     border-radius:6px;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums;text-align:right}
  .series{font-family:"SFMono-Regular",Consolas,"Liberation Mono",monospace;
          font-size:.92rem;background:#0f1c33;color:#e7eefb;padding:12px 14px;
          border-radius:10px;overflow-x:auto;white-space:nowrap}
  .series .lead{color:#ffd166;font-weight:700}
  .verdict{display:inline-block;padding:3px 11px;border-radius:999px;
           font-size:.82rem;font-weight:700}
  .yes{background:#e3f5ec;color:var(--good)}
  .no{background:#fdeaea;color:var(--hot)}
  .fibres{position:relative;height:104px;margin-top:6px}
  .tick{position:absolute;bottom:26px;width:2px;background:#b9c6d8}
  .tick.here{background:var(--hot);width:5px}
  .tick.ker{background:var(--good);width:5px}
  .tlabel{position:absolute;bottom:4px;transform:translateX(-50%);
          font-size:.78rem;color:var(--muted)}
  .marker{position:absolute;transform:translateX(-50%);font-size:.78rem;
          color:var(--accent);font-weight:700}
  .axis{position:absolute;bottom:26px;left:0;right:0;height:1px;background:#c8d3e2}
  .note{font-size:.88rem;color:var(--muted);margin-top:.6rem}
  code{background:#eef3fa;padding:1px 5px;border-radius:4px;font-size:.88em}
  .grid2{display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;gap:18px}
  @media(max-width:820px){.grid2{grid-template-columns:1fr}}
  button{background:var(--accent);color:#fff;border:0;padding:7px 14px;
         border-radius:8px;font-size:.88rem;cursor:pointer}
  button.ghost{background:#eef3fa;color:var(--accent)}
  button:hover{filter:brightness(1.08)}
</style>
</head>
<body>
<div class="wrap">
  <h1>The Pole-Order Laboratory</h1>
  <p class="sub">
    A <em>normalized</em> series is one of the shape
    <b>f = q<sup>−1</sup> + a + b q + c q<sup>2</sup> + …</b> —
    a simple pole with residue exactly 1. Multiply several of them and watch what
    happens to the pole. Every number below is computed exactly, with integer arithmetic.
  </p>

  <div class="card">
    <h2>1  Choose how many factors</h2>
    <div class="row">
      <div>
        <label for="mSlider">number of normalized factors  <b>m</b></label><br>
        <input type="range" id="mSlider" min="0" max="8" value="3">
      </div>
      <div><span class="big" id="mOut">3</span></div>
      <div>
        <button class="ghost" id="randBtn">randomize coefficients</button>
        <button class="ghost" id="moonBtn">use moonshine data</button>
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="note">
      The <em>moonshine data</em> button loads genuine linear coefficients
      c<sub>g</sub>(1) of McKay–Thompson series for the Monster classes
      1A, 2A, 2B, 3A, 4A, 5A — that is 196884, 4372, −276, 783, 276, 134,
      each of the form 1 + χ(g) for the 196883-dimensional character — together
      with the full expansions
      <b>J = q<sup>−1</sup> + 196884 q + 21493760 q<sup>2</sup> + …</b>
      and <b>q<sup>−1</sup> + 4372 q + 96256 q<sup>2</sup> + …</b>
      for the first two. Every such series has vanishing constant term; the remaining
      rows start at zero and are yours to edit.
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <h2>2  Edit the factors</h2>
    <table id="facTable">
      <thead><tr><th>factor</th><th>a<sub>i</sub> (constant)</th><th>b<sub>i</sub> (coeff of q)</th><th>c<sub>i</sub> (coeff of q<sup>2</sup>)</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody></tbody>
    </table>
    <div class="note">Each row is <code>q^-1 + a + b q + c q²</code>. The coefficient of
    <code>q^-1</code> is locked at 1 — that is what "normalized" means.</div>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <h2>3  The product</h2>
    <div class="series" id="prodOut"></div>
    <div class="row" style="margin-top:12px">
      <div>order of the product:  <span class="big" id="ordOut"></span></div>
      <div>leading coefficient:  <span class="big" id="lcOut"></span></div>
      <div>is it normalized?  <span id="normOut"></span></div>
      <div>is it a power series?  <span id="psOut"></span></div>
    </div>
    <div class="note" id="poleNote"></div>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <h2>4  Repair the pole</h2>
    <div class="row">
      <div>
        <label for="kSlider">multiply by  q<sup><b id="kLab">0</b></sup></label><br>
        <input type="range" id="kSlider" min="0" max="16" value="0">
      </div>
      <div>resulting order:  <span class="big" id="kOrd"></span></div>
      <div><span id="kVerdict"></span></div>
    </div>
    <div class="series" id="corrOut" style="margin-top:12px"></div>
    <div class="note" id="unitNote"></div>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <h2>5  Where the product lives</h2>
    <p class="note" style="margin-top:0">
      The order is a group homomorphism from the nonzero Laurent series onto the
      integers. Its fibres are disjoint, so the integer below decides <em>completely</em>
      whether the product can be normalized (fibre −1) or a unit power series (fibre 0).
    </p>
    <div class="fibres" id="fibres"></div>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <h2>6  The coefficients just past the pole</h2>
    <div class="grid2">
      <div>
        <table>
          <tr><th>quantity</th><th>from the product</th><th>predicted</th></tr>
          <tr><td>coefficient of q<sup>1−m</sup></td><td id="l1a"></td><td id="l1b"></td></tr>
          <tr><td>2 × coefficient of q<sup>2−m</sup></td><td id="l2a"></td><td id="l2b"></td></tr>
        </table>
        <div class="note">
          Level 1: the coefficient one step above the pole is
          <b>∑<sub>i</sub> a<sub>i</sub></b>.<br>
          Level 2: <b>2c = 2∑<sub>i</sub> b<sub>i</sub> + (∑<sub>i</sub> a<sub>i</sub>)² − ∑<sub>i</sub> a<sub>i</sub>²</b>,
          i.e. <b>∑ b<sub>i</sub> + e<sub>2</sub>(a)</b> with e<sub>2</sub> the second
          elementary symmetric function — Newton's identity in disguise.
        </div>
      </div>
      <div>
        <div class="note" style="margin-top:0">
          <b>Why these identities exist.</b> Every normalized f factors uniquely as
          <b>q<sup>−1</sup> u</b> with u a power series of constant term 1.
          So a product of m of them is <b>q<sup>−m</sup> u<sub>1</sub>…u<sub>m</sub></b>,
          and its coefficient at q<sup>k−m</sup> is just the coefficient at
          q<sup>k</sup> of a product of power series all starting with 1 — which is
          exactly where elementary symmetric functions come from.
        </div>
        <div id="symOut" class="series" style="margin-top:10px"></div>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

<script>
// ---------- exact truncated Laurent arithmetic over the integers (BigInt) ----
const WIN = 8;                    // coefficient window length
function mul(f, g){               // f = {v, c:[BigInt]}
  const n = Math.min(f.c.length, g.c.length);
  const out = new Array(n).fill(0n);
  for(let i=0;i<n;i++){
    if(f.c[i]===0n) continue;
    for(let j=0;i+j<n;j++) out[i+j] += f.c[i]*g.c[j];
  }
  return {v: f.v+g.v, c: out};
}
function one(){ const c=new Array(WIN).fill(0n); c[0]=1n; return {v:0,c}; }
function shift(f,k){ return {v:f.v+k, c:f.c.slice()}; }
function coeff(f,n){ const j=n-f.v; return (j>=0&&j<f.c.length)?f.c[j]:0n; }
function order(f){ for(let j=0;j<f.c.length;j++) if(f.c[j]!==0n) return f.v+j; return null; }
function normalized(a,b,c){ const arr=new Array(WIN).fill(0n); arr[0]=1n;
  arr[1]=BigInt(a); arr[2]=BigInt(b); arr[3]=BigInt(c); return {v:-1,c:arr}; }
function fmt(x){ return x.toString().replace(/\B(?=(\d{3})+(?!\d))/g, "\u2009"); }
function render(f, highlightLead){
  const parts=[];
  for(let j=0;j<f.c.length;j++){
    const a=f.c[j]; if(a===0n) continue;
    const e=f.v+j;
    let t = (a===1n && e!==0) ? "" : (a===-1n && e!==0 ? "-" : fmt(a));
    if(e===0) t = fmt(a);
    else if(e===1) t += "q";
    else t += "q<sup>"+e+"</sup>";
    parts.push(parts.length===0 && highlightLead ? '<span class="lead">'+t+'</span>' : t);
  }
  return (parts.length?parts.join("  +  "):"0") + "  +  …";
}

// ---------- state -----------------------------------------------------------
const MOON = [[0,196884,21493760],[0,4372,96256],[0,-276,0],[0,783,0],
              [0,276,0],[0,134,0],[0,0,0],[0,0,0]];
let m = 3;
let data = [];
function reseed(kind){
  data = [];
  for(let i=0;i<8;i++){
    if(kind==="moon") data.push(MOON[i].slice());
    else data.push([Math.floor(Math.random()*21)-10,
                    Math.floor(Math.random()*81)-40,
                    Math.floor(Math.random()*161)-80]);
  }
}
reseed("moon");

// ---------- UI --------------------------------------------------------------
const $ = id => document.getElementById(id);
function buildTable(){
  const tb = $("facTable").querySelector("tbody");
  tb.innerHTML = "";
  for(let i=0;i<m;i++){
    const tr = document.createElement("tr");
    tr.innerHTML = "<td>f<sub>"+(i+1)+"</sub></td>";
    for(let k=0;k<3;k++){
      const td=document.createElement("td");
      const inp=document.createElement("input");
      inp.type="number"; inp.value=data[i][k];
      inp.addEventListener("input", ()=>{ data[i][k]=parseInt(inp.value||"0",10); update(); });
      td.appendChild(inp); tr.appendChild(td);
    }
    tb.appendChild(tr);
  }
}
function fibrePanel(ord){
  const host=$("fibres"); host.innerHTML="";
  const lo=-9, hi=3;
  const ax=document.createElement("div"); ax.className="axis"; host.appendChild(ax);
  for(let d=lo; d<=hi; d++){
    const x = ((d-lo)/(hi-lo))*100;
    const t=document.createElement("div");
    t.className="tick"+(d===-1?" here":(d===0?" ker":""));
    t.style.left=x+"%"; t.style.height=(d===-1||d===0)?"52px":"30px";
    host.appendChild(t);
    const l=document.createElement("div"); l.className="tlabel";
    l.style.left=x+"%"; l.textContent=d; host.appendChild(l);
  }
  const put=(d,txt,top)=>{ if(d<lo||d>hi) return;
    const x=((d-lo)/(hi-lo))*100; const e=document.createElement("div");
    e.className="marker"; e.style.left=x+"%"; e.style.top=top+"px";
    e.innerHTML=txt; host.appendChild(e); };
  put(-1,"normalized",0);
  put(0,"units of ℂ[[q]]",18);
  if(ord!==null) put(ord,"● your product ("+ord+")",40);
}
function update(){
  $("mOut").textContent = m;
  let P = one();
  for(let i=0;i<m;i++) P = mul(P, normalized(data[i][0],data[i][1],data[i][2]));
  const ord = order(P), lc = ord===null?0n:coeff(P,ord);
  $("prodOut").innerHTML = render(P,true);
  $("ordOut").textContent = ord===null?"\u221e":ord;
  $("lcOut").textContent = lc.toString();
  const isNorm = (m===1);
  $("normOut").innerHTML = isNorm ? '<span class="verdict yes">yes — only when m = 1</span>'
                                  : '<span class="verdict no">no</span>';
  $("psOut").innerHTML = (m===0) ? '<span class="verdict yes">yes (empty product = 1)</span>'
                                 : '<span class="verdict no">no — genuine pole</span>';
  $("poleNote").innerHTML = "The order is exactly −m = −"+m+
    ", and the leading coefficient is exactly 1. Poles add with no cancellation, "+
    "because the coefficient field has no zero divisors: the product of the leading "+
    "coefficients 1·1·…·1 can never be zero.";

  const k = parseInt($("kSlider").value,10);
  $("kLab").textContent = k;
  const Q = shift(P,k), qo = order(Q);
  $("kOrd").textContent = qo===null?"\u221e":qo;
  $("kVerdict").innerHTML = (qo===0)
      ? '<span class="verdict yes">order 0 — and k = m is the only exponent that does this</span>'
      : '<span class="verdict no">not yet order 0</span>';
  $("corrOut").innerHTML = render(Q, qo===0);
  $("unitNote").innerHTML = (qo===0)
    ? "Its constant term is 1, so this is not merely a power series — it is an "+
      "<b>invertible</b> one, a unit of the power series ring. The corrected product "+
      "lands in the group of principal units 1 + qℂ[[q]]."
    : "Slide k until the order hits 0. There is exactly one value that works, namely k = m = "+m+".";

  fibrePanel(ord);

  // Newton identities
  let p1=0n,p2=0n,sb=0n;
  for(let i=0;i<m;i++){ const a=BigInt(data[i][0]); p1+=a; p2+=a*a; sb+=BigInt(data[i][1]); }
  const l1 = coeff(P,1-m), l2 = 2n*coeff(P,2-m);
  const l1p = p1, l2p = 2n*sb + p1*p1 - p2;
  $("l1a").textContent=fmt(l1); $("l1b").textContent=fmt(l1p);
  $("l2a").textContent=fmt(l2); $("l2b").textContent=fmt(l2p);
  const e2 = (p1*p1-p2)/2n;
  $("symOut").innerHTML = "p₁ = ∑a<sub>i</sub> = "+fmt(p1)+
      "    p₂ = ∑a<sub>i</sub>² = "+fmt(p2)+
      "    e₂(a) = (p₁² − p₂)/2 = "+fmt(e2);
}
$("mSlider").addEventListener("input", e=>{ m=parseInt(e.target.value,10); buildTable(); update(); });
$("kSlider").addEventListener("input", update);
$("randBtn").addEventListener("click", ()=>{ reseed("rand"); buildTable(); update(); });
$("moonBtn").addEventListener("click", ()=>{ reseed("moon"); buildTable(); update(); });
buildTable(); update();
</script>
</body>
</html>
"
    },
    {
      "title": "The 194 Chamber: Building a Monster-Sized Pole One Conjugacy Class at a Time",
      "description": "An explorer for the full Monstrous Moonshine product. A single slider runs from 0 to 194, the number of conjugacy classes of the Monster, and at each step multiplies in one more normalized trace series, recomputing the entire leading window of the product in exact big-integer arithmetic. The display shows the pole deepening by exactly one order per class, the leading coefficient staying pinned at 1, the unique correction exponent q^n tracking the count, and the verdict that the product is never a power series. A coefficient table contrasts the computed coefficients at degrees -n, 1-n and 2-n with the theoretical predictions: the sum of the factors' constant terms at level 1 and the sum of their linear terms plus the second elementary symmetric function at level 2. A toggle deliberately breaks the moonshine normalization by giving the first series a nonzero constant term, so the reader can watch the subleading coefficient stop vanishing and understand exactly which hypothesis was doing the work. At two factors the display reads 196884 + 4372 = 201256, the two numbers that opened moonshine.",
      "html": "<!DOCTYPE html>

<style>

<body>
<div class="wrap">
  <h1>The 194 Chamber</h1>
  <p class="sub">
    The Monster simple group has exactly <b>194</b> conjugacy classes, and Monstrous
    Moonshine attaches to each one a trace series
    <b>T<sub>g</sub> = q<sup>−1</sup> + c<sub>g</sub>(1) q + c<sub>g</sub>(2) q<sup>2</sup> + …</b>
    Every one of them has the same simple pole. Multiply them and watch the pole deepen,

      <div class="box"><div class="k">unique correction</div><div class="v" id="corr"></div></div>
      <div class="box"><div class="k">is it a power series?</div><div class="v hot" id="ps"></div></div>

    <div class="note" id="note"></div>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <h2>The first three coefficients, and what they know</h2>
    <table>
      <tr><th>degree</th><th>coefficient of the product</th><th>what the theory predicts</th></tr>
      <tr><td id="d0">q<sup>−n</sup></td><td id="c0"></td><td>1, always</td></tr>
      <tr><td id="d1">q<sup>1−n</sup></td><td id="c1"></td><td id="p1"></td></tr>
      <tr><td id="d2">q<sup>2−n</sup></td><td id="c2"></td><td id="p2"></td></tr>
    </table>
    <div class="note" id="expl"></div>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <h2>Where the numbers come from</h2>
    <div class="note" style="margin-top:0">
      The genuine coefficients loaded here are
      c<sub>1A</sub>(1) = 196884, c<sub>2A</sub>(1) = 4372, c<sub>2B</sub>(1) = −276,
      c<sub>3A</sub>(1) = 783, c<sub>4A</sub>(1) = 276, c<sub>5A</sub>(1) = 134 — each of
      the form 1 + χ(g), where χ is the 196883-dimensional character of the Monster,
      which is why 196884 = 196883 + 1 and 4372 = 4371 + 1. The remaining classes are filled
      with fixed illustrative values of the same shape; the theorems on display depend only on
      the shape <b>q<sup>−1</sup> + 0 + c(1)q + …</b>, not on the particular numbers.
    </div>

<script>
const WIN = 5;
const REAL = [196884, 4372, -276, 783, 276, 134];
// deterministic illustrative fill for the remaining classes
const C1 = [];
for(let i=0;i<194;i++){
  if(i < REAL.length) C1.push(REAL[i]);
  else { const x = ((i*i*7919 + 104729) % 20011) - 6000; C1.push(x); }
}
const C2 = [21493760, 96256, 0, 0, 0, 0];

function mul(f,g){
  const n = Math.min(f.c.length, g.c.length);
  const out = new Array(n).fill(0n);
  for(let i=0;i<n;i++){ if(f.c[i]===0n) continue;
    for(let j=0;i+j<n;j++) out[i+j] += f.c[i]*g.c[j]; }
  return {v:f.v+g.v, c:out};
}
function fac(i, a0){
  const c = new Array(WIN).fill(0n);
  c[0]=1n; c[1]=BigInt(a0); c[2]=BigInt(C1[i]); c[3]=BigInt(i<C2.length?C2[i]:0);
  return {v:-1,c};
}
function coeff(f,n){ const j=n-f.v; return (j>=0&&j<f.c.length)?f.c[j]:0n; }
function fmt(x){ return x.toString().replace(/\B(?=(\d{3})+(?!\d))/g,"\u2009"); }

const $ = id=>document.getElementById(id);

function update(){
  const n = parseInt($("n").value,10);
  const broken = $("breakNorm").checked;
