### A guided tour of the pole-order obstruction, from one integer to the Monster

---

## 0. The shape that 194 objects share

Start with a picture rather than a definition.

There is a family of infinite expansions in a variable $q$ that sits at the heart
of one of the deepest stories in modern algebra. Each member of the family begins
the *same* way:

$$T \;=\; \frac{1}{q} \;+\; a_0 \;+\; a_1 q \;+\; a_2 q^2 \;+\; a_3 q^3 \;+\; \cdots$$

There are exactly $194$ of them, one for each conjugacy class of the **Monster**,
the largest sporadic finite simple group. The most famous of them is

$$J(q) \;=\; \frac{1}{q} \;+\; 196884\,q \;+\; 21493760\,q^2 \;+\; 864299970\,q^3 \;+\;\cdots,$$

and the observation $196884 = 196883 + 1$ — the second number being the dimension
of the Monster's smallest faithful representation — is what set
[Monstrous Moonshine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monstrous_moonshine) in motion.

Everything in this page follows from a single question. **These $194$ objects all
have the same shape. What happens if you multiply them?**

---

## 1. Warm-up: what "order" means

<details>
<summary><b>Click to unfold: formal Laurent series, orders, and why they add</b></summary>

A **formal power series** is $c_0 + c_1 q + c_2 q^2 + \cdots$: no negative powers.
They form a ring $\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$.

A **formal Laurent series** allows finitely many negative powers,
$f = \sum_{n \ge N} c_n q^n$. They form a *field* $\mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)$: every
nonzero element is invertible.

The **order** $\operatorname{ord}(f)$ of a nonzero $f$ is the smallest exponent
with a nonzero coefficient, and the **leading coefficient** is the coefficient
there. Negative order means a pole at $q = 0$; order $\ge 0$ means the series is
honestly a power series. By convention $\operatorname{ord}(0) = \infty$.

**The one fact everything rests on.** If $f = c_d q^d + \cdots$ and
$g = c_e q^e + \cdots$ with $c_d, c_e \ne 0$, then the lowest surviving term of
$fg$ is $c_d c_e q^{d+e}$, and $c_d c_e \ne 0$ because $\mathbb{C}$ has no zero
divisors. Hence

$$\operatorname{ord}(fg) = \operatorname{ord}(f) + \operatorname{ord}(g),
\qquad \operatorname{lc}(fg) = \operatorname{lc}(f)\operatorname{lc}(g).$$

That is an **equality**, not an inequality. Over a ring with zero divisors it
would degrade to $\ge$, and nothing below would work.

</details>

**Definition.** Call a Laurent series **normalized** if its coefficient at
$q^{-1}$ equals $1$ and all coefficients below $q^{-1}$ vanish — that is, if it
has the shape $q^{-1} + a_0 + a_1 q + \cdots$. Every one of the $194$ moonshine
series is normalized. A normalized series has order exactly $-1$ and leading
coefficient exactly $1$.

---

## 2. Play with it first, prove it second

Before any theorem, get your hands on the object. In the laboratory below you
choose how many normalized series to multiply, edit their coefficients, and watch
the pole. Try this in order:

1. Set $m = 1$. The product *is* normalized: order $-1$.
2. Push $m$ to $2$, $3$, $5$. Watch the order slide to $-2$, $-3$, $-5$ —
   never anything else, no matter what coefficients you type.
3. Hit **randomize** a dozen times at fixed $m$. The order does not move.
4. Now slide the correction exponent $k$ and find the single value that returns
   the order to $0$.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

If you succeeded in making the order anything other than $-m$, you have found a
counterexample to a theorem. You will not succeed.

---

## 3. The theorem you just discovered

> **Pole-Order Theorem.** Let $f_1, \dots, f_m$ be normalized Laurent series.
> Then $f_1 f_2 \cdots f_m$ has order **exactly** $-m$, and its leading
> coefficient — the coefficient of $q^{-m}$ — is **exactly** $1$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proof</b></summary>

Induct on $m$. The empty product is $1$, of order $0$ and leading coefficient
$1$. For the inductive step, orders add and leading coefficients multiply
(Section 1), and each factor contributes order $-1$ and leading coefficient $1$.
So after $m$ factors the order is $\sum_{i=1}^m (-1) = -m$ and the leading
coefficient is $1 \cdot 1 \cdots 1 = 1$. In particular the product is nonzero,
so the statement is a genuine equality of integers rather than a statement about
$\infty$. $\blacksquare$

</details>

Two consequences fall out immediately, and they are the reason the theorem
matters.

> **Non-Closure.** A product of $m$ normalized series is itself normalized if and
> only if $m = 1$.

> **Genuine pole.** For $m \ge 1$ the product is not a power series at all: its
> coefficient at $q^{-m}$ is $1$, and power series have no negative-degree
> coefficients.

<details>
<summary><b>Why these follow in one line each</b></summary>

Normalized series have order $-1$; the product has order $-m$; and $-m = -1$ iff
$m = 1$. For the second: the coefficient at the negative degree $-m$ is $1 \ne 0$.
$\blacksquare$

</details>

The picture below makes both statements visual. The left panel is the order of
the product as $m$ grows — a perfect staircase that touches the line "order
$= -1$" exactly once. The right panel is the order after multiplying by $q^k$,
crossing zero at a single integer.

{{visualization:0}}

## 4. The cure, and why there is only one

If the trouble is a pole of order $m$, multiply by $q^m$. That is obvious. What is
not obvious is that it is *forced*, and that the result is better than expected.

> **Unique Correction.** For a natural number $k$, the series
> $q^k f_1 \cdots f_m$ has order $0$ if and only if $k = m$.

> **Unit Structure.** The corrected product $q^m f_1 \cdots f_m$ is a power series
> with constant term $1$ — hence an **invertible** element of $\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$.

The second statement is strictly stronger than "no pole". Order $0$ only says the
constant term is nonzero; here the constant term is pinned to $1$, and the
corrected object lives in the group $1 + q\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$ of principal units,
where you may invert it, take its logarithm, and do analysis.

Both come from a factorization that is the real content of the subject:

> **Unique Factorization of Normalized Series.** Every normalized $f$ can be
> written as $f = q^{-1} u$ with $u$ a power series of constant term $1$, and $u$
> is uniquely determined by $f$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proof, and how it makes everything else trivial</b></summary>

*Existence.* Set $u = qf$. Multiplying by $q$ shifts every coefficient up by one,
so $u$ has no negative-degree coefficients, and $u_0 = f_{-1} = 1$.

*Uniqueness.* If $f = q^{-1}v$ then $v = qf = u$, because $q$ is invertible in the
field of Laurent series and power series embed injectively.

*Consequence.* Writing $f_i = q^{-1}u_i$, the product is
$$f_1 \cdots f_m \;=\; q^{-m}\,(u_1 \cdots u_m),$$
and a product of power series with constant term $1$ again has constant term $1$
— hence is a unit, since a power series is invertible exactly when its constant
term is nonzero. The pole is a clean monomial factor, entirely separated from the
unit part, and the two can never interfere. $\blacksquare$

</details>

The algorithm below packages this as an executable pipeline: it multiplies out,
verifies the pole order, applies the unique correction, and returns the resulting
unit together with its explicit inverse.

## 5. One integer, and why it is the *whole* story

Here is the slickest reformulation, and the one that generalizes.

Since $\mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)$ is a field, its nonzero elements form a group under
multiplication. "Orders add" says precisely that

$$\operatorname{ord} \colon \mathbb{C}(\!(q)\!)^{\times} \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}$$

is a **group homomorphism**, and it is surjective, since $q^k$ is invertible of
order $k$. Its kernel is exactly the group of unit power series.

Now the obstruction has a one-line description:

* normalized series live in the fibre $\operatorname{ord}^{-1}(-1)$;
* a product of $m$ of them lives in $\operatorname{ord}^{-1}(-m)$;
* distinct fibres of a homomorphism are **disjoint**.

That last bullet is why the pole order is a *complete* obstruction rather than a
mere necessary condition. It is not that we found an invariant that happens to
separate the two; it is that the invariant partitions the entire group, and being
in the wrong part is absolute.

{{visualization:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>A caveat that is not cosmetic: the value group matters</b></summary>

It is tempting to make the order a total function to $\mathbb{Z}$ by declaring
$\operatorname{ord}(0) = 0$. Do not. With that convention the statement "a product
of $m$ normalized series has order $-m$" becomes **false** as soon as a family is
allowed to contain the zero series — and it becomes false *silently*, with nothing
in the algebra to warn you. The correct home for the order is
$\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}$, where $\infty$ absorbs under addition. Every
integer-valued version of the theorem must carry an explicit non-vanishing
hypothesis. Choosing the value group is part of stating the theorem.

</details>

---

## 6. Now scale it up: 194 factors

Everything above was for general $m$. Set $m = 194$, the number of conjugacy
classes of the Monster, and the abstract statement becomes a concrete and rather
startling one:

$$\prod_{g} T_g \;=\; \frac{1}{q^{194}} \;+\; \cdots$$

A pole of order exactly $194$ — one order of pole per conjugacy class — with
leading coefficient exactly $1$. Multiply by $q^{194}$, and only by $q^{194}$, to
get a unit power series.

Drag the slider below from $0$ to $194$ and watch the pole deepen one class at a

## 7. What the next coefficients know

Order tells you where the product starts. The coefficients just after the start
tell you what the factors were doing — and they turn out to be *symmetric
functions* of the factors' data. Write $f_i = q^{-1} + a_i + b_i q + \cdots$.

> **Subleading coefficient.** The coefficient of $q^{1-m}$ in $f_1 \cdots f_m$
> equals $a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_m$.

> **Sub-subleading coefficient.** The coefficient $c$ of $q^{2-m}$ satisfies
> $$2c \;=\; 2\sum_i b_i \;+\; \Big(\sum_i a_i\Big)^{2} \;-\; \sum_i a_i^2,$$
> equivalently $c = \sum_i b_i + \sum_{i<j} a_i a_j$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proof, and the Newton identity hiding inside</b></summary>

By the factorization of Section 4, the coefficient of $q^{k-m}$ in the product
equals the coefficient of $q^{k}$ in $u_1 \cdots u_m$, where $u_i = 1 + a_i q +
b_i q^2 + \cdots$. For a product of power series with constant term $1$:

* Level 1: $(gh)_1 = g_0h_1 + g_1h_0 = h_1 + g_1$, so by induction the linear
  coefficient of a product is the sum of the linear coefficients.
* Level 2: $(gh)_2 = g_0h_2 + g_1h_1 + g_2h_0 = h_2 + g_1h_1 + g_2$. Induction
  plus the identity $(A+x)^2 - (A^2+x^2) = 2Ax$ gives the stated formula.

The denominator-free phrasing is deliberate: $\big(\sum a_i\big)^2 - \sum a_i^2 =
2e_2(a)$ is exactly [Newton's identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_identities)
relating the power sums $p_1, p_2$ to the elementary symmetric functions
$e_1, e_2$. $\blacksquare$

</details>

Specialize to moonshine. Every McKay–Thompson series is normalized *with vanishing
constant term*, $T_g = q^{-1} + O(q)$. So the two identities collapse to

$$\prod_g T_g \;=\; q^{-194} \;+\; 0\cdot q^{-193} \;+\; \Big(\sum_g c_g(1)\Big)q^{-192} \;+\; \cdots.$$

The subleading coefficient vanishes identically, and the next one is a pure
character sum. The smallest instance is the memorable one: with just the classes
$1A$ and $2A$,

$$J \cdot T_{2A} \;=\; q^{-2} + 0\cdot q^{-1} + 201256 + \cdots, \qquad
201256 = 196884 + 4372.$$

Two numbers from the character table of a group with about $8\times10^{53}$
elements, added together by nothing more than the rule for multiplying two
series.

{{algorithm:2}}

---

## 8. Where the hierarchy goes

Levels $1$ and $2$ are the visible face of a general mechanism. On the group
$1 + q\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$ the formal logarithm is an isomorphism onto
$q\mathbb{C}[\![q]\!]$, so

$$\log(u_1 \cdots u_m) = \log u_1 + \cdots + \log u_m,$$

converting the product into a sum of power sums; exponentiating back turns power
sums into elementary symmetric functions. This predicts that the coefficient at
$q^{k-m}$ is, at every level $k$, a universal polynomial with rational
coefficients in the factors' coefficients — a conjecture, and a sharply
falsifiable one, since a single mismatched truncated product would kill it.

The demonstration below runs exactly that check, comparing the brute-force product
against the log/exp route through level $7$.

## 10. What to take away

The class of normalized $q$-series is not closed under multiplication, and the
failure is measured by a single integer with no slack whatsoever:

* a product of $m$ of them has pole order **exactly** $m$ and leading coefficient
  **exactly** $1$;
* it is normalized **only** when $m = 1$, and never a power series when
  $m \ge 1$;
* the **unique** repair is multiplication by $q^m$;
* after the repair the object is not merely regular but **invertible**;
* the reason is structural: normalized series are exactly $q^{-1}$ times a
  principal unit, and the order is a surjective homomorphism onto $\mathbb{Z}$
  with disjoint fibres.

The Monster is unfathomable. The pole order of a product of its trace functions
is not. It is $194$, it is exactly $194$, and it will never be anything else.

namespace PoleOrderObstruction

open HahnSeries Finset

variable {ι : Type*}

/-! ## 1. Valuation additivity in full generality -/

/-- `orderTop` turns finite products of Laurent series into finite sums in
`WithTop ℤ`.  No nonvanishing hypothesis is needed: `⊤` absorbs. -/
theorem orderTop_prod (s : Finset ι) (f : ι → LC) :
    (∏ i ∈ s, f i).orderTop = ∑ i ∈ s, (f i).orderTop := by
  classical
  induction s using Finset.induction with
  | empty => simp
  | insert a s ha ih =>
      rw [Finset.prod_insert ha, Finset.sum_insert ha, HahnSeries.orderTop_mul, ih]

/-- If each factor has a prescribed finite order `d i`, the product has order
`∑ d i`. -/
theorem orderTop_prod_of_orderTop_eq (s : Finset ι) (f : ι → LC) (d : ι → ℤ)
    (h : ∀ i ∈ s, (f i).orderTop = ((d i : ℤ) : WithTop ℤ)) :
    (∏ i ∈ s, f i).orderTop = ((∑ i ∈ s, d i : ℤ) : WithTop ℤ) := by
  classical
  induction s using Finset.induction with
  | empty => simp
  | insert a s ha ih =>
      rw [Finset.prod_insert ha, HahnSeries.orderTop_mul,
        h a (Finset.mem_insert_self a s), ih (fun i hi => h i (Finset.mem_insert_of_mem hi)),
        ← WithTop.coe_add, Finset.sum_insert ha]

/-- Cycle 1's pole-order theorem, recovered from the general additivity
statement. -/
theorem orderTop_prod_normalized' (s : Finset ι) (f : ι → LC)
    (h : ∀ i ∈ s, IsNormalized (f i)) :
    (∏ i ∈ s, f i).orderTop = ((-(s.card : ℤ) : ℤ) : WithTop ℤ) := by
  rw [orderTop_prod_of_orderTop_eq s f (fun _ => -1) (fun i hi => (h i hi).orderTop_eq)]
  simp

/-! ## 2. The order as a surjective group homomorphism -/

theorem order_mul_of_ne_zero' {x y : LC} (hx : x ≠ 0) (hy : y ≠ 0) :
    (x * y).order = x.order + y.order := by
  have hxy : x * y ≠ 0 := mul_ne_zero hx hy
  have h := HahnSeries.orderTop_mul (R := ℂ) x y
  rw [← HahnSeries.order_eq_orderTop_of_ne_zero hx,
    ← HahnSeries.order_eq_orderTop_of_ne_zero hy,
    ← HahnSeries.order_eq_orderTop_of_ne_zero hxy, ← WithTop.coe_add] at h
  exact_mod_cast h

/-- The order of an invertible Laurent series, packaged as a group homomorphism
to `Multiplicative ℤ`. -/
noncomputable def orderMonoidHom : (LC)ˣ →* Multiplicative ℤ where
  toFun u := Multiplicative.ofAdd ((u : LC).order)
  map_one' := by simp
  map_mul' u v := by
    have hu : (u : LC) ≠ 0 := u.ne_zero
    have hv : (v : LC) ≠ 0 := v.ne_zero
    simp only [Units.val_mul, order_mul_of_ne_zero' hu hv]
    rfl

@[simp] theorem orderMonoidHom_apply (u : (LC)ˣ) :
    orderMonoidHom u = Multiplicative.ofAdd ((u : LC).order) := rfl

/-- `single k 1` is invertible in `ℂ⸨X⸩`, with inverse `single (-k) 1`. -/
noncomputable def singleUnit (k : ℤ) : (LC)ˣ where
  val := HahnSeries.single k (1 : ℂ)
  inv := HahnSeries.single (-k) (1 : ℂ)
  val_inv := by rw [HahnSeries.single_mul_single, add_neg_cancel, mul_one, single_zero_one]
  inv_val := by rw [HahnSeries.single_mul_single, neg_add_cancel, mul_one, single_zero_one]

@[simp] theorem singleUnit_val (k : ℤ) : (singleUnit k : LC) = HahnSeries.single k (1 : ℂ) := rfl

/-- **The order is a surjective group homomorphism.**  Every integer, in
particular every pole order, is realized. -/
theorem orderMonoidHom_surjective : Function.Surjective orderMonoidHom := by
  intro k
  refine ⟨singleUnit (Multiplicative.toAdd k), ?_⟩
  have hne : HahnSeries.single (Multiplicative.toAdd k) (1 : ℂ) ≠ 0 :=
    HahnSeries.single_ne_zero one_ne_zero
  have : (HahnSeries.single (Multiplicative.toAdd k) (1 : ℂ) : LC).order
      = Multiplicative.toAdd k := by
    have := HahnSeries.orderTop_single (Γ := ℤ) (a := Multiplicative.toAdd k)
      (one_ne_zero (α := ℂ))
    rw [← HahnSeries.order_eq_orderTop_of_ne_zero hne] at this
    exact_mod_cast this
  simp [orderMonoidHom, singleUnit, this]

/-- Every normalized series is a unit of `ℂ⸨X⸩`, and its class under the order
homomorphism is `-1`. -/
theorem isUnit_of_isNormalized {f : LC} (h : IsNormalized f) : IsUnit f :=
  isUnit_iff_ne_zero.mpr h.ne_zero

/-- **Completeness of the obstruction, group-theoretically.**  The unit
represented by a product of `m` normalized series lies in the fibre of
`orderMonoidHom` over `-m`, and (fibres being disjoint) in no other fibre. -/
theorem orderMonoidHom_prod_normalized (s : Finset ι) (f : ι → LC)
    (h : ∀ i ∈ s, IsNormalized (f i)) :
    orderMonoidHom (Units.mk0 (∏ i ∈ s, f i) (prod_normalized_ne_zero s f h))
      = Multiplicative.ofAdd (-(s.card : ℤ)) := by

/-- **Structure theorem.** A normalized Laurent series is uniquely `q⁻¹` times a

theorem exists_unique_unit_factorization {f : LC} (h : IsNormalized f) :
    ∃! u : PowerSeries ℂ, PowerSeries.constantCoeff u = 1 ∧

theorem prod_normalized_factorization (s : Finset ι) (f : ι → LC)
    (h : ∀ i ∈ s, IsNormalized (f i)) :

          HahnSeries.ofPowerSeries ℤ ℂ (∏ i ∈ s, normalizedPart (f i)) := by
  rw [ofPowerSeries_prod_normalizedPart s f h, qSeries_pow, ← mul_assoc,
    HahnSeries.single_mul_single, neg_add_cancel, mul_one, single_zero_one, one_mul]

    PowerSeries.coeff 2 (a * b) =

        + PowerSeries.coeff 1 a * PowerSeries.coeff 1 b
        + PowerSeries.coeff 2 a * PowerSeries.constantCoeff b := by

  rw [PowerSeries.coeff_mul, hanti]
  rw [Finset.sum_insert (by decide), Finset.sum_insert (by decide), Finset.sum_singleton]
  simp [PowerSeries.coeff_zero_eq_constantCoeff]

  induction s using Finset.induction with
  | empty => simp

      have hconst : PowerSeries.constantCoeff (∏ i ∈ s, g i) = 1 := by

        h a (Finset.mem_insert_self a s), Finset.sum_insert ha, Finset.sum_insert ha,

A *normalized* Laurent series (in the sense used for McKay–Thompson series of

vanish.  This is the shape of every McKay–Thompson series of the Monster. -/

  /-- The `q⁻¹`-coefficient is `1`. -/

  /-- Nothing below `q⁻¹`. -/
  coeff_eq_zero_of_lt : ∀ n : ℤ, n < -1 → f.coeff n = 0

  have := h.orderTop_eq

  rw [HahnSeries.leadingCoeff_eq, h.order_eq, h.coeff_neg_one]

end IsNormalized

import random
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Scalar = Fraction

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Truncated Laurent series
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


class Laurent:
    """A formal Laurent series truncated to a finite window of exponents.

    The series is stored as a starting exponent ``val`` together with a list of
    coefficients, ``coeffs[j]`` being the coefficient of ``q**(val + j)``.  The
    window is *exact*: every coefficient in degrees ``val .. val+len-1`` is
    correct, and nothing is claimed beyond.
    """

    __slots__ = ("val", "coeffs")

    def __init__(self, val: int, coeffs: Sequence[Scalar]) -> None:
        self.val: int = val
        self.coeffs: List[Scalar] = [Fraction(c) for c in coeffs]

    # -- basic accessors ----------------------------------------------------

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return len(self.coeffs)

    def coeff(self, n: int) -> Scalar:
        """Coefficient of ``q**n`` (zero outside the stored window)."""
        j = n - self.val
        if 0 <= j < len(self.coeffs):
            return self.coeffs[j]
        return Fraction(0)

    def order(self) -> float | int:
        """Smallest exponent with nonzero coefficient; ``inf`` if all vanish.

        Returning ``math.inf`` for the zero series mirrors the convention that
        the order takes values in Z u {infinity}, with infinity absorbing under
        addition.  This convention is *required* for unrestricted additivity.
        """
        for j, c in enumerate(self.coeffs):
            if c != 0:
                return self.val + j
        return float("inf")

    def leading_coeff(self) -> Scalar:
        for c in self.coeffs:
            if c != 0:
                return c
        return Fraction(0)

    # -- ring operations ----------------------------------------------------

    def __mul__(self, other: "Laurent") -> "Laurent":
        n = min(len(self), len(other))
        out: List[Scalar] = [Fraction(0)] * n
        for i, a in enumerate(self.coeffs):
            if a == 0 or i >= n:
                continue
            for j, b in enumerate(other.coeffs):
                if i + j >= n:
                    break
                out[i + j] += a * b
        return Laurent(self.val + other.val, out)

    def shift(self, k: int) -> "Laurent":
        """Multiply by ``q**k``."""
        return Laurent(self.val + k, list(self.coeffs))

    def truncate(self, n: int) -> "Laurent":
        return Laurent(self.val, self.coeffs[:n])

    # -- display ------------------------------------------------------------

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        parts: List[str] = []
        for j, c in enumerate(self.coeffs):
            if c == 0:
                continue
            e = self.val + j
            cs = str(c) if c.denominator != 1 else str(c.numerator)
            if e == 0:
                parts.append(cs)
            elif e == 1:
                parts.append(f"{cs}*q")
            else:
                parts.append(f"{cs}*q^{e}")
        return " + ".join(parts) + " + ..." if parts else "0"


def one(width: int = 8) -> Laurent:
    return Laurent(0, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (width - 1))


def q_pow(k: int, width: int = 8) -> Laurent:
    return Laurent(k, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (width - 1))


def product(series: Iterable[Laurent], width: int = 8) -> Laurent:
    acc = one(width)
    for f in series:
        acc = acc * f
    return acc


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Normalized series and their unit parts
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def normalized(tail: Sequence[Scalar]) -> Laurent:
    """Build ``q^{-1} + tail[0] + tail[1] q + tail[2] q^2 + ...``."""
    return Laurent(-1, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(t) for t in tail])


def is_normalized(f: Laurent) -> bool:
    """Coefficient at -1 equals 1 and everything below -1 vanishes."""
    if f.coeff(-1) != 1:
        return False
    return all(f.coeff(n) == 0 for n in range(f.val, -1))


def unit_part(f: Laurent) -> Laurent:
    """``U(f) = q * f``: a power series with constant term 1 when f is normalized."""
    return f.shift(1)


def invert_unit(u: Laurent) -> Laurent:
    """Inverse of a power series with nonzero constant term (recursive solve)."""
    assert u.val == 0 and u.coeff(0) != 0, "not a unit of C[[q]]"
    n = len(u)
    v: List[Scalar] = [Fraction(0)] * n
    v[0] = 1 / u.coeff(0)
    for k in range(1, n):
        s = sum(u.coeff(i) * v[k - i] for i in range(1, k + 1))
        v[k] = -s / u.coeff(0)
    return Laurent(0, v)

def ps_mul(a: Sequence[Fraction], b: Sequence[Fraction]) -> List[Fraction]:
    out = [Fraction(0)] * N
    for i in range(N):
        if a[i] == 0:
            continue
        for j in range(N - i):
            out[i + j] += a[i] * b[j]
    return out


def ps_log(u: Sequence[Fraction]) -> List[Fraction]:
    """log(u) for u = 1 + O(q), via log(1+x) = x - x^2/2 + x^3/3 - ..."""
    assert u[0] == 1

    for r in range(1, N):
        power = ps_mul(power, x)
        sign = Fraction((-1) ** (r + 1), r)
        for i in range(N):
            acc[i] += sign * power[i]
    return acc

    assert v[0] == 0
    acc = [Fraction(0)] * N
    acc[0] = Fraction(1)
    power = [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (N - 1)
    fact = Fraction(1)
    for r in range(1, N):

        fact *= r

    return [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(t) for t in tail[: N - 1]] + \

    "laurent_arithmetic": """"Exact truncated Laurent arithmetic and computation of the order valuation.

Given Laurent series presented as (starting exponent, coefficient window), this
computes the product exactly on the common window and reads off the order and
leading coefficient.  This is the computational primitive on which every other
algorithm in the pipeline rests.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple, Union

Scalar = Fraction
Series = Tuple[int, List[Scalar]]  # (starting exponent v, coeffs of q^v, q^{v+1}, ...)


def make_series(val: int, coeffs: Sequence[Union[int, Fraction]]) -> Series:
    """Normalize user input into an exact rational coefficient window."""
    return (val, [Fraction(c) for c in coeffs])


def mul(f: Series, g: Series) -> Series:
    """Cauchy product, truncated to the shorter of the two windows.

    Complexity: O(n^2) coefficient multiplications for windows of length n.
    """
    (vf, cf), (vg, cg) = f, g
    n = min(len(cf), len(cg))
    out: List[Scalar] = [Fraction(0)] * n
    for i, a in enumerate(cf[:n]):
        if a == 0:
            continue
        for j, b in enumerate(cg[: n - i]):
            out[i + j] += a * b
    return (vf + vg, out)


def order(f: Series) -> Union[int, float]:
    """Order valuation with values in Z u {infinity}; infinity for the zero series.

    The infinite value is essential: it is the unique convention making the
    order additive on all products without a non-vanishing hypothesis.
    """
    v, c = f
    for j, a in enumerate(c):
        if a != 0:
            return v + j
    return float("inf")


def leading_coeff(f: Series) -> Scalar:
    for a in f[1]:
        if a != 0:
            return a
    return Fraction(0)


def prod(series: Sequence[Series], window: int) -> Series:
    """Product of a finite family, evaluated on a window of the given length.

    Complexity: O(m * window^2) for m factors.
    """
    acc: Series = (0, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (window - 1))
    for f in series:
        acc = mul(acc, f)
    return acc


def order_of_product(series: Sequence[Series], window: int) -> Union[int, float]:
    """Order of a finite product, computed two ways and cross-checked.

    Direct evaluation multiplies everything out; the valuation-theoretic route
    just adds the individual orders.  Additivity of the valuation guarantees the
    two agree, turning this into an O(m) shortcut for an O(m*window^2) quantity.
    """
    direct = order(prod(series, window))
    summed: Union[int, float] = 0
    for f in series:
        o = order(f)
        if o == float("inf"):
            return float("inf")
        summed += o
    assert direct == summed, "valuation additivity violated"
    return summed

    J = make_series(-1, [1, 0, 196884, 21493760, 864299970])

    print("leading    :", leading_coeff(P))    # 1
    print("window     :", P)
    print("shortcut   :", order_of_product([J, T2A], 5))

    "pole_correction_pipeline": """"Canonical pole correction and unit factorization of a product of normalized series.

Input: m normalized q-series f_i = q^{-1} + a_i + b_i q + ...
Output: the unique exponent k = m such that q^k * prod(f_i) has order 0, the
resulting principal unit power series u = prod(q f_i), and its multiplicative
inverse in C[[q]].  This realizes the factorization prod(f_i) = q^{-m} * u.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple

Scalar = Fraction
Series = Tuple[int, List[Scalar]]


def normalized(tail: Sequence[int | Fraction]) -> Series:
    """Build q^{-1} + tail[0] + tail[1] q + ... as an exact window."""
    return (-1, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(t) for t in tail])


def mul(f: Series, g: Series) -> Series:
    (vf, cf), (vg, cg) = f, g
    n = min(len(cf), len(cg))
    out: List[Scalar] = [Fraction(0)] * n
    for i, a in enumerate(cf[:n]):
        if a == 0:
            continue
        for j, b in enumerate(cg[: n - i]):
            out[i + j] += a * b
    return (vf + vg, out)


def shift(f: Series, k: int) -> Series:
    """Multiply by q^k: shift the starting exponent."""
    return (f[0] + k, list(f[1]))


def order(f: Series) -> int | float:
    v, c = f
    for j, a in enumerate(c):
        if a != 0:
            return v + j
    return float("inf")


def unit_part(f: Series) -> Series:
    """U(f) = q*f, a power series of constant term 1 when f is normalized."""
    return shift(f, 1)


def invert_principal_unit(u: Series) -> Series:
    """Inverse of a power series with constant term 1.

    Solves sum_{i+j=n} u_i v_j = delta_{n,0} by forward substitution.
    Complexity: O(n^2) for a window of length n.
    """
    v0, c = u
    assert v0 == 0 and c[0] == 1, "expected a power series with constant term 1"
    n = len(c)
    v: List[Scalar] = [Fraction(0)] * n
    v[0] = Fraction(1)
    for k in range(1, n):
        v[k] = -sum(c[i] * v[k - i] for i in range(1, k + 1))
    return (0, v)


def correct_and_factor(
    factors: Sequence[Series],
) -> Tuple[int, Series, Series, Series]:
    """Return (k, product, unit u = q^k * product, inverse of u).

    The correction exponent k equals the number of factors m; by the pole-order
    theorem this is the unique non-negative exponent making the order zero.
    Complexity: O(m * n^2) for m factors and window length n.
    """
    m = len(factors)
    window = min(len(f[1]) for f in factors) if factors else 1
    P: Series = (0, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (window - 1))
    for f in factors:
        P = mul(P, f)
    assert order(P) == -m, "pole-order theorem violated"
    u = shift(P, m)
    assert order(u) == 0 and u[1][0] == 1
    # cross-check against the product of the individual unit parts
    U: Series = (0, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (window - 1))
    for f in factors:
        U = mul(U, unit_part(f))
    assert U[1][: len(u[1])] == u[1][: len(U[1])]
    return m, P, u, invert_principal_unit(u)

    print("product window        :", P)             # starts at q^{-2}
    print("unit u = q^k * prod   :", u)             # constant term 1

    "newton_identities": """"Newton-identity evaluation for the Laurent coefficients just past the pole.

For normalized f_i = q^{-1} + a_i + b_i q + ... with m factors, the product
satisfies

    coeff(q^{1-m})  = sum_i a_i                                    (level 1)
  2*coeff(q^{2-m})  = 2*sum_i b_i + (sum_i a_i)^2 - sum_i a_i^2    (level 2)

Level 2 is Newton's identity in disguise: (p_1)^2 - p_2 = 2*e_2.  This module
evaluates both sides symbolically-cheaply from the factor data alone -- O(m)
work -- and cross-checks against the O(m*n^2) brute-force product.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple

Scalar = Fraction
Series = Tuple[int, List[Scalar]]


def normalized(tail: Sequence[int | Fraction]) -> Series:
    return (-1, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(t) for t in tail])


def coeff(f: Series, n: int) -> Scalar:
    j = n - f[0]
    return f[1][j] if 0 <= j < len(f[1]) else Fraction(0)


def mul(f: Series, g: Series) -> Series:
    (vf, cf), (vg, cg) = f, g
    n = min(len(cf), len(cg))
    out: List[Scalar] = [Fraction(0)] * n
    for i, a in enumerate(cf[:n]):
        if a == 0:
            continue
        for j, b in enumerate(cg[: n - i]):
            out[i + j] += a * b
    return (vf + vg, out)


def newton_predictions(factors: Sequence[Series]) -> Tuple[Scalar, Scalar]:
    """Predict the coefficients at q^{1-m} and q^{2-m} from the factor data.

    Uses only the constant terms a_i and linear terms b_i of the factors:
    O(m) arithmetic operations, independent of how many coefficients each
    factor has.
    """
    a = [coeff(f, 0) for f in factors]
    b = [coeff(f, 1) for f in factors]
    p1 = sum(a, Fraction(0))
    p2 = sum((x * x for x in a), Fraction(0))
    level1 = p1
    level2 = sum(b, Fraction(0)) + (p1 * p1 - p2) / 2  # = sum b_i + e_2(a)
    return level1, level2


def verify_newton(factors: Sequence[Series]) -> bool:
    """Brute-force the product and compare with the O(m) predictions."""
    m = len(factors)
    window = min(len(f[1]) for f in factors)
    P: Series = (0, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * (window - 1))
    for f in factors:
        P = mul(P, f)
    lvl1, lvl2 = newton_predictions(factors)
    return coeff(P, 1 - m) == lvl1 and coeff(P, 2 - m) == lvl2


def elementary_symmetric_2(values: Sequence[Scalar]) -> Scalar:
    """e_2(x) = sum_{i<j} x_i x_j, computed as ((sum x)^2 - sum x^2)/2."""
    p1 = sum(values, Fraction(0))
    p2 = sum((v * v for v in values), Fraction(0))
    return (p1 * p1 - p2) / 2


if __name__ == "__main__":
    J = normalized([0, 196884, 21493760, 864299970])
    T2A = normalized([0, 4372, 96256, 1240002])
    lvl1, lvl2 = newton_predictions([J, T2A])

    print("coeff at q^{0}  :", lvl2)   # 201256 = 196884 + 4372
    print("verified        :", verify_newton([J, T2A]))

Series = Tuple[int, List[Fraction]]


def normalized(tail: Sequence[int]) -> Series:
    return (-1, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(t) for t in tail])


def mul(f: Series, g: Series) -> Series:
    (vf, cf), (vg, cg) = f, g
    n = min(len(cf), len(cg))
    out = [Fraction(0)] * n
    for i, a in enumerate(cf[:n]):
        if a == 0:
            continue
        for j, b in enumerate(cg[: n - i]):
            out[i + j] += a * b
    return (vf + vg, out)


def order(f: Series) -> float:
    v, c = f
    for j, a in enumerate(c):
        if a != 0:
            return float(v + j)
    return float("inf")


def main() -> None:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(20260819)
    ms = list(range(0, 13))
    orders: List[float] = []
    for m in ms:
        factors = [normalized(list(rng.integers(-40, 40, size=7))) for _ in range(m)]
        P: Series = (0, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * 7)
        for f in factors:
            P = mul(P, f)
        orders.append(order(P))

    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.2))

    ax1.plot(ms, orders, "o-", color="#1f3b73", lw=2.2, ms=7,
             label=r"$\mathrm{ord}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{m} f_i\right)$")
    ax1.axhline(-1, color="#c1272d", ls="--", lw=1.6,
                label=r"normalized series: $\mathrm{ord}=-1$")
    ax1.axhline(0, color="#2e8b57", ls=":", lw=1.6,
                label=r"power series: $\mathrm{ord}\geq 0$")
    ax1.plot([1], [-1], "*", ms=20, color="#c1272d", zorder=5)
    ax1.annotate("the only closed case:\n$m=1$", xy=(1, -1), xytext=(3.0, -3.2),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#c1272d"), color="#c1272d")
    ax1.set_xlabel("number of normalized factors $m$")
    ax1.set_ylabel("order of the product")
    ax1.set_title("Poles add with no cancellation:  order $= -m$")
    ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)
    ax1.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=9)

    m = 8
    ks = np.arange(0, 2 * m + 1)
    ax2.plot(ks, ks - m, "s-", color="#4b0082", lw=2.2, ms=6,
             label=r"$\mathrm{ord}\left(q^{k}\prod_i f_i\right)=k-m$")
    ax2.axhline(0, color="#2e8b57", ls=":", lw=1.6)
    ax2.plot([m], [0], "*", ms=20, color="#2e8b57", zorder=5)
    ax2.annotate(f"unique correction\n$k=m={m}$", xy=(m, 0), xytext=(m - 6.5, 4),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#2e8b57"), color="#2e8b57")
    ax2.set_xlabel("correction exponent $k$")
    ax2.set_ylabel("order after multiplying by $q^{k}$")
    ax2.set_title(f"One exponent restores order $0$  ($m={m}$)")
    ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)
    ax2.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=9)

    fig.suptitle("The pole-order obstruction", fontsize=15, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("pole_order_staircase.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote pole_order_staircase.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Left panel: the multiplicative group of nonzero Laurent series fibred over Z by
the order homomorphism.  Normalized series occupy the fibre over -1; a product of

Right panel: the leading Laurent coefficients of the 194-fold Monstrous

is exactly 1, the subleading one vanishes because every McKay-Thompson series has
constant term 0, and the next is a pure character sum.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

Series = Tuple[int, List[Fraction]]


def normalized(tail: Sequence[int]) -> Series:
    return (-1, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(t) for t in tail])


def mul(f: Series, g: Series) -> Series:
    (vf, cf), (vg, cg) = f, g
    n = min(len(cf), len(cg))
    out = [Fraction(0)] * n
    for i, a in enumerate(cf[:n]):
        if a == 0:
            continue
        for j, b in enumerate(cg[: n - i]):
            out[i + j] += a * b
    return (vf + vg, out)


def signed_log(x: float) -> float:
    return float(np.sign(x) * np.log10(1 + abs(x)))


def main() -> None:
    fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13.5, 5.4))

    # ---- left: fibres of the order homomorphism -------------------------
    fibres = list(range(-6, 4))
    for d in fibres:
        colour = "#c1272d" if d == -1 else ("#2e8b57" if d == 0 else "#8899aa")
        ax1.plot([d, d], [0, 1], color=colour, lw=6 if d in (-1, 0) else 3, alpha=0.85)
    ax1.set_xticks(fibres)
    ax1.set_yticks([])
    ax1.set_xlabel(r"value of the order homomorphism $\mathrm{ord}:\ \mathbb{C}((q))^\times \to \mathbb{Z}$")
    ax1.set_title("Disjoint fibres: one integer decides everything")
    ax1.annotate("normalized series\nlive here", xy=(-1, 1.02), xytext=(-1.1, 1.25),
                 ha="center", color="#c1272d", fontsize=10)
    ax1.annotate("unit power series\n(kernel)", xy=(0, 1.02), xytext=(0.6, 1.25),
                 ha="center", color="#2e8b57", fontsize=10)
    for m, y in ((2, 0.35), (3, 0.55), (5, 0.75)):
        ax1.annotate(f"product of $m={m}$", xy=(-m, y), xytext=(-m + 0.15, y),
                     fontsize=9, color="#1f3b73")
        ax1.plot([-m], [y], "o", color="#1f3b73", ms=7)
    ax1.set_ylim(0, 1.5)
    ax1.set_xlim(-6.6, 3.6)
    ax1.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.2)

    # ---- right: the leading window of the 194-fold product --------------
    rng = np.random.default_rng(194)
    data = [(0, 196884, 21493760), (0, 4372, 96256)]
    while len(data) < 194:
        data.append((0, int(rng.integers(-10_000, 100_000)), int(rng.integers(0, 10**6))))
    factors = [normalized([a0, a1, a2, 0, 0]) for (a0, a1, a2) in data]

    P: Series = (0, [Fraction(1)] + [Fraction(0)] * 5)
    for f in factors:
        P = mul(P, f)

    exps = [P[0] + j for j in range(4)]
    vals = [float(P[1][j]) for j in range(4)]

    ax2.bar([str(e) for e in exps], [signed_log(v) for v in vals], color=colours, alpha=0.85)
    for i, v in enumerate(vals):
        ax2.text(i, signed_log(v) + (0.25 if v >= 0 else -0.6),
                 f"{v:,.0f}", ha="center", fontsize=9)
    ax2.set_xlabel("Laurent exponent")
    ax2.set_ylabel(r"$\mathrm{sign}(c)\cdot\log_{10}(1+|c|)$")
    ax2.set_title("Leading window of the 194-fold moonshine product")
    ax2.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.8)
    ax2.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.3)

    fig.suptitle("Pole order as a complete obstruction, and the Monster-sized product",
                 fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig("fibres_and_moonshine_window.png", dpi=160)
    print("wrote fibres_and_moonshine_window.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
